    25	grazed grassland. Its tributaries have failed their nutrient standards in every
    26	classification since 2015, mainly because nitrate and phosphorus are washed from fields and
    27	released where livestock have direct access to the channel. Riparian buffers, strips of
    28	permanent vegetation between farmland and the stream, are widely promoted as a low-cost
    29	remedy because they intercept runoff, take up nutrients, stabilise banks and shade the
    30	water. Their performance in practice varies a great deal, however, and few schemes have been
    31	monitored for long enough, or against suitable controls, to separate the effect of the
    32	buffer from changes in weather and farming.
    33	In 2021 the Partnership agreed to fund buffer planting on six tributary reaches and asked
    34	the Trust to find out whether water quality and stream ecology improved as a result. This
    35	report presents the full four years of monitoring. It addresses three questions: whether
    36	nutrient concentrations and turbidity fell at restored reaches relative to controls; whether
    37	conditions for stream invertebrates improved; and whether the response depended on the width
    38	of the buffer.
    39	2 Previous studies
    40	Published evaluations report a wide range of outcomes. In a review of 38 buffer schemes in
    41	temperate Europe, Ostrander and Vey (2018) found a median nitrate reduction of 33% in
    42	shallow groundwater beneath buffers but only 12% in the receiving streams. On the Kell
    43	Water, nitrate-N fell from 6.1 to 4.9 mg/L in the ten years after a 15-metre grass buffer
    44	was established, a reduction of 20%, with no change in total phosphorus (Brennan and
    45	colleagues, 2017). Wooded buffers in the Ardle uplands, by contrast, reduced total
    46	phosphorus by 27% within three years (Haldane and Pike, 2020).
    47	Shading effects are better established. Summer maximum water temperatures beneath a mature
    48	riparian canopy are typically 2 to 4 °C lower than in open reaches (Maddox, 2015), and newly
    49	planted buffers have lowered summer maxima by 0.8 °C within five years (Ferrar and Quine,
    50	2021). Invertebrate responses tend to lag behind chemical change: Ostrander and Vey (2018)
    51	reported that community index scores rose by 0.4 points on average, and only in schemes more
    52	than five years old. Several authors conclude that buffers narrower than 10 metres deliver
    53	little benefit for nitrate (Brennan and colleagues, 2017; Okoro, 2019).

    55	3 Methods
    56	3.1 Study reaches
    57	Twelve reaches, each 500 metres long, were selected on eight first- and second-order
    58	tributaries. Six were restored and six served as controls. Control reaches were matched to
    59	restored reaches on upstream catchment area, share of grazed grassland and baseline nitrate
    60	concentration, and none was fenced or planted during the study. At restored reaches,
    61	livestock were excluded with post-and-wire fencing, and the strip between the fence and the
    62	bank top was planted at 2,500 trees per hectare with alder, willow, hawthorn and oak. Buffer
    63	width, measured from bank top to fence, ranged from 10 to 30 metres and was set by the
    64	amount of land each farmer was willing to release (Table 1).

    66	Reach group Reaches Buffer width (m) Upstream catchment (ha) Grazed grassland (%)
    67	Restored, buffer 20 m or wider 4 20 to 30 640 68
    68	Restored, buffer under 20 m 2 10 to 12 550 71
    69	Control 6 none 600 69
    70	3.2 Sampling and laboratory analysis
    71	Spot water samples were taken monthly at the downstream end of every reach, giving 48
    72	sampling occasions per reach over the four years. Automatic samplers collected additional
    73	samples during up to six storm events per reach each year. Nitrate-N and total phosphorus
    74	were analysed by the Trust's accredited laboratory, and turbidity was measured in the field
    75	with a calibrated probe. Duplicate samples and field blanks were analysed with every batch,
    76	and all batches met the laboratory's acceptance criteria. Temperature loggers recorded water
    77	temperature every 15 minutes from May to September. Macroinvertebrates were sampled each
    78	October with a three-minute kick sample and scored on the community index used by the
    79	regional regulator, on which higher scores indicate cleaner water.

    82	means for each reach were analysed with a linear mixed model with reach as a random effect
    83	and period (before or after), group (restored or control) and their interaction as fixed
    84	effects. The interaction term is the BACI effect: the change at restored reaches over and
    85	above the change at control reaches. Group means are reported with the p-value for the
    86	interaction, and p < 0.05 was taken as significant. Because only two restored reaches had
    87	buffers narrower than 20 metres, the comparison between wide and narrow buffers is
    88	descriptive.

    92	2023, when flooding prevented access to four reaches. Rainfall in 2024 was 9% above the
    93	long-term average, while 2021 was close to average. Mean flows in 2024 were about 12% higher
    94	than in 2021 at restored and control reaches alike, so dilution does not explain the
    95	difference between the two groups. Table 2 summarises the main water-quality variables for
    96	the baseline and final years.

    98	Mean nitrate-N at restored reaches fell from 4.6 mg/L in 2021 to 3.5 mg/L in 2024, a
    99	reduction of 24%. At control reaches, mean nitrate-N changed little, falling 5% from 4.4 to
   100	4.2 mg/L. The BACI interaction was significant (p = 0.01). Most of the reduction occurred
   101	between 2022 and 2023, as the planted trees became established.
   102	Table 2. Annual mean water quality at restored and control reaches, 2021 and 2024.
   103	Variable Restored 2021 Restored 2024 Control 2021 Control 2024 BACI p
   104	Nitrate-N (mg/L) 4.6 3.5 4.4 4.2 0.01

   108	December and February when field drains run most strongly. The gap between restored and
   109	control reaches was widest in these winter months and narrowest in late summer, when
   110	concentrations in both groups were lowest. In every month of 2024, concentrations at
   111	restored reaches were below those at control reaches.

   113	4.2 Phosphorus and turbidity
   114	Total phosphorus fell by 19% at restored reaches, from 0.118 to 0.096 mg/L, compared with a
   115	10% fall at control reaches, from 0.112 to 0.101 mg/L. The largest decreases at restored
   116	reaches came in winter, when trampling of banks by livestock had previously been greatest.

   118	significant (p = 0.21), and phosphorus concentrations in both groups remained above the
   119	standard for good status.

   121	from 46 to 29 NTU at restored reaches and from 44 to 39 NTU at control reaches (p = 0.04).

   123	of the six restored reaches.

   125	Loggers were fixed in shaded pools at the downstream end of each reach, about 30 centimetres
   126	below the surface. Loggers at two control reaches failed in July 2021 and were replaced
   127	within three weeks, and the gaps were not infilled. Summer water temperatures for the two
   128	groups of reaches are summarised in Table 3.
   129	Table 3. Mean summer maximum water temperature (°C), May to September.
   130	Reach group 2021 2022 2023 2024
   131	Restored 19.8 19.5 18.7 18.1
   132	Control 19.6 20.1 19.4 19.9
   133

   136	October 2024, while the score at control reaches moved from 5.0 to 5.1 (BACI p = 0.03). This
   137	effect was confined to the four reaches with buffers at least 20 metres wide, with no change
   138	at the two narrow-buffer reaches. Mayfly and caddisfly families that are sensitive to
   139	pollution were recorded in 2024 at three restored reaches where none had been found in 2021.

   141	Buffer width made a marked difference to the nitrate response. At the four reaches with
   142	buffers 20 metres or wider, mean nitrate-N fell by 31%, from 4.55 to 3.15 mg/L, whereas at
   143	the two narrow-buffer reaches, with buffers of 10 and 12 metres, it fell by only 11%, from
   144	4.70 to 4.20 mg/L. With only two narrow-buffer reaches, this comparison is descriptive and
   145	was not tested statistically. Values for individual reaches are given in the accompanying
   146	spreadsheet.

   148	Woodland buffers produced a clear reduction in nitrate at restored reaches relative to
   149	controls within three years of planting. The size of the reduction is at the upper end of
   150	the range reported for receiving streams in the studies reviewed in Section 2, probably
   151	because the Halden scheme combined livestock exclusion with dense tree planting rather than
   152	grass alone. The temperature results in Table 3 are notable given that the trees were less
   153	than four metres tall in 2024, and shading should increase as the canopy closes.

   156	sediment and moves during storms, so annual means of monthly spot samples are a noisy

results.answer:
The Halden Vale buffer monitoring found that riparian woodland buffers plus livestock exclusion improved stream conditions over three years, especially where buffers were at least 20 metres wide.

Main findings:
- Nitrate fell at restored reaches from 4.6 to 3.5 mg/L, a 24% drop, while controls changed little; the BACI effect was significant.
- Total phosphorus also fell at restored reaches, but the difference versus controls was not statistically significant.
- Storm-event turbidity declined more clearly at restored reaches, from 46 to 29 NTU, and this was significant.
- Mean summer water temperatures were lower at restored reaches by 2024.
- Macroinvertebrate community scores improved at restored reaches, but this response was confined to the wider buffers.

The report’s key practical conclusion is that buffers of 20 metres or more performed best, with nearly three times the nitrate reduction of the 10–12 metre buffers, though the report says that width result should be confirmed before being treated as a firm minimum standard.

ANSWER: Halden Vale’s buffer monitoring found that native woodland riparian buffers with livestock exclusion reduced nitrate, lowered storm turbidity, slightly improved ecology, and likely cooled streams, with the strongest benefits coming from buffers at least 20 metres wide.

The Halden Vale monitoring found that the riparian woodland buffers were associated with improved water quality and ecology at the restored stream reaches compared with matched controls.

Key findings:
- **Nitrate fell clearly at restored reaches**: mean nitrate-N dropped from **4.6 mg/L in 2021 to 3.5 mg/L in 2024**, while controls changed only from **4.4 to 4.2 mg/L**. The BACI effect was significant (**p = 0.01**).
- **Phosphorus declined, but less clearly**: total phosphorus fell from **0.118 to 0.096 mg/L** at restored reaches, versus **0.112 to 0.101 mg/L** at controls, but this was **not statistically significant** (**p = 0.21**).
- **Storm turbidity improved**: median storm turbidity dropped from **46 to 29 NTU** at restored reaches, compared with **44 to 39 NTU** at controls (**p = 0.04**).
- **Water temperature was lower at restored reaches** by 2024: summer maximum temperature fell to **18.1 °C** at restored reaches, while controls were **19.9 °C**.
- **Macroinvertebrates improved**: the community index rose from **4.9 to 5.6** at restored reaches, compared with **5.0 to 5.1** at controls (**BACI p = 0.03**).

The report says the **strongest responses were at buffers 20 metres wide or more**:
- Nitrate fell by **31%** at the wider buffers, but only **11%** at the **10- and 12-metre** buffers.
- The wider buffers were also the ones where invertebrate scores improved.

Overall conclusion:
- **Native woodland buffers combined with livestock exclusion reduced nitrate within three years**, reduced storm sediment/turbidity, and improved stream ecology.
- The report recommends **widening the two narrow buffers to at least 20 metres**, continuing monitoring to **2027**, and adding more storm-event phosphorus sampling.

ANSWER: Halden Vale’s buffer restoration reduced nitrate significantly, lowered storm turbidity, improved stream invertebrates, and likely helped cool the water; phosphorus also fell but not significantly. The best results were at buffers at least 20 metres wide, so the report recommends widening the narrower buffers to at least 20 metres.

   138	at the two narrow-buffer reaches. Mayfly and caddisfly families that are sensitive to
   139	pollution were recorded in 2024 at three restored reaches where none had been found in 2021.
   140	4.5 Influence of buffer width
   141	Buffer width made a marked difference to the nitrate response. At the four reaches with
   142	buffers 20 metres or wider, mean nitrate-N fell by 31%, from 4.55 to 3.15 mg/L, whereas at
   143	the two narrow-buffer reaches, with buffers of 10 and 12 metres, it fell by only 11%, from
   144	4.70 to 4.20 mg/L. With only two narrow-buffer reaches, this comparison is descriptive and
   145	was not tested statistically. Values for individual reaches are given in the accompanying
   146	spreadsheet.
   147	5 Discussion
   148	Woodland buffers produced a clear reduction in nitrate at restored reaches relative to
   149	controls within three years of planting. The size of the reduction is at the upper end of
   150	the range reported for receiving streams in the studies reviewed in Section 2, probably
   151	because the Halden scheme combined livestock exclusion with dense tree planting rather than
   152	grass alone. The temperature results in Table 3 are notable given that the trees were less
   153	than four metres tall in 2024, and shading should increase as the canopy closes.
   154	
   155	The phosphorus results are less conclusive. Phosphorus in these streams is mostly bound to
   156	sediment and moves during storms, so annual means of monthly spot samples are a noisy
   157	measure of it, and the significant fall in storm turbidity suggests that sediment delivery
   158	did decline. The invertebrate response appeared sooner than the literature led us to expect,
   159	although only at the wider buffers.
   160	For catchment managers, the most practical finding concerns width. Buffers of 20 metres or
   161	more achieved nearly three times the nitrate reduction of the 10- and 12-metre buffers, and
   162	only the wider buffers improved invertebrate scores. Because farmers chose the width, the
   163	wider buffers may also sit on land with different drainage, so this pattern should be
   164	confirmed before it is used to set a minimum width.
   165	6 Limitations
   166	The study has several limitations. Reaches were not randomly assigned to restoration: they
   167	were chosen where farmers volunteered land, and restored and control reaches may differ in
   168	ways the matching did not capture. With six reaches per group, the study had limited power
   169	to detect moderate effects, which matters for the phosphorus result. Monthly spot sampling
   170	under-represents storm flows, when most phosphorus and sediment are transported. Three
   171	post-planting years are too few to capture the full effect of canopy closure. Finally, the
   172	study did not survey fish, measure groundwater, or record changes in fertiliser use on the
   173	surrounding farms.
   174	7 Conclusions and recommendations
   175	Native woodland buffers combined with livestock exclusion reduced nitrate in Halden
   176	tributaries within three years, and buffers at least 20 metres wide performed best. We
   177	recommend that the Partnership widen the two narrow buffers to at least 20 metres, continue
   178	monitoring until 2027 to capture the effect of canopy closure, and add storm-event
   179	phosphorus sampling at all restored reaches.
   180	
   181	Acknowledgements

   183	Riverwatch who helped with invertebrate sampling, and the Trust's laboratory staff. Planting
   184	was funded by the Halden Catchment Partnership with a grant from the Lowland Streams Fund.
   185	Data availability
   186	Monthly results for every reach are held by the Trust and are available to Partnership
   187	members on request. Annual mean nitrate-N for each reach in 2021 and 2024 is provided in the
   188	accompanying spreadsheet.

   193	stream temperature. River Restoration Review 8, 45-57.

results.answer:
The Halden Vale buffer monitoring found that the restored riparian woodland buffers, combined with keeping livestock out, improved stream conditions over the 2021–2024 period.

Main findings:
- Nitrate-N fell at restored reaches from 4.6 mg/L to 3.5 mg/L, a 24% reduction, while control reaches changed only slightly. This was statistically significant.
- Total phosphorus also fell at restored reaches, from 0.118 to 0.096 mg/L, but the difference versus controls was not statistically significant.
- Storm-event turbidity improved, dropping from 46 to 29 NTU at restored reaches; this was significant.
- Water temperature was lower at restored reaches by 2024, though the report presents this mainly as a positive trend rather than a statistical result.
- Macroinvertebrate scores improved at restored reaches, rising from 4.9 to 5.6, again significantly.
- Buffer width mattered: reaches with buffers 20 metres or wider showed much stronger nitrate reductions and better invertebrate responses than the 10–12 metre buffers.

Overall conclusion:
- The report says native woodland buffers are effective for reducing nitrate in these lowland livestock tributaries, especially when buffers are at least 20 metres wide.
- It recommends widening the two narrow buffers, continuing monitoring to 2027, and adding more storm-event phosphorus sampling.

ANSWER: The monitoring found that Halden Vale’s restored woodland buffers, especially those at least 20 metres wide, reduced nitrate and storm turbidity, improved macroinvertebrate scores, and likely helped lower water temperature; phosphorus fell too, but that result was less clear statistically.

The report gives two different nitrate-drop figures for the restored (buffered) reaches:

- **31%** in the **Abstract**
- **24%** in **Section 4.1 / Table 2** (`4.6` to `3.5 mg/L`)

So for a slide, the safest wording is that nitrate **fell by 24% in the results, while the abstract summarizes it as 31%**. ANSWER: The report is inconsistent: it says nitrate fell by **31%** in the abstract, but **24%** in the results for the restored reaches.

   107	Nitrate concentrations at all reaches followed the usual seasonal cycle, peaking between
   108	December and February when field drains run most strongly. The gap between restored and
   109	control reaches was widest in these winter months and narrowest in late summer, when
   110	concentrations in both groups were lowest. In every month of 2024, concentrations at
   111	restored reaches were below those at control reaches.
   112	
   113	4.2 Phosphorus and turbidity
   114	Total phosphorus fell by 19% at restored reaches, from 0.118 to 0.096 mg/L, compared with a
   115	10% fall at control reaches, from 0.112 to 0.101 mg/L. The largest decreases at restored
   116	reaches came in winter, when trampling of banks by livestock had previously been greatest.
   117	However, the difference between restored and control reaches was not statistically
   118	significant (p = 0.21), and phosphorus concentrations in both groups remained above the
   119	standard for good status.
   120	Storm-event turbidity responded more clearly. Median turbidity during sampled storms fell
   121	from 46 to 29 NTU at restored reaches and from 44 to 39 NTU at control reaches (p = 0.04).
   122	Before fencing, bank poaching by cattle was the main visible source of fine sediment at four
   123	of the six restored reaches.
   124	4.3 Water temperature
   125	Loggers were fixed in shaded pools at the downstream end of each reach, about 30 centimetres
   126	below the surface. Loggers at two control reaches failed in July 2021 and were replaced
   127	within three weeks, and the gaps were not infilled. Summer water temperatures for the two
   128	groups of reaches are summarised in Table 3.
   129	Table 3. Mean summer maximum water temperature (°C), May to September.
   130	Reach group 2021 2022 2023 2024
   131	Restored 19.8 19.5 18.7 18.1
   132	Control 19.6 20.1 19.4 19.9

   134	4.4 Macroinvertebrates
   135	The mean community index score at restored reaches rose from 4.9 in October 2021 to 5.6 in
   136	October 2024, while the score at control reaches moved from 5.0 to 5.1 (BACI p = 0.03). This
   137	effect was confined to the four reaches with buffers at least 20 metres wide, with no change
   138	at the two narrow-buffer reaches. Mayfly and caddisfly families that are sensitive to
   139	pollution were recorded in 2024 at three restored reaches where none had been found in 2021.
   140	4.5 Influence of buffer width
   141	Buffer width made a marked difference to the nitrate response. At the four reaches with
   142	buffers 20 metres or wider, mean nitrate-N fell by 31%, from 4.55 to 3.15 mg/L, whereas at
   143	the two narrow-buffer reaches, with buffers of 10 and 12 metres, it fell by only 11%, from
   144	4.70 to 4.20 mg/L. With only two narrow-buffer reaches, this comparison is descriptive and
   145	was not tested statistically. Values for individual reaches are given in the accompanying
   146	spreadsheet.
   147	5 Discussion
   148	Woodland buffers produced a clear reduction in nitrate at restored reaches relative to
   149	controls within three years of planting. The size of the reduction is at the upper end of
   150	the range reported for receiving streams in the studies reviewed in Section 2, probably
   151	because the Halden scheme combined livestock exclusion with dense tree planting rather than
   152	grass alone. The temperature results in Table 3 are notable given that the trees were less
   153	than four metres tall in 2024, and shading should increase as the canopy closes.
   154	
   155	The phosphorus results are less conclusive. Phosphorus in these streams is mostly bound to
   156	sediment and moves during storms, so annual means of monthly spot samples are a noisy
   157	measure of it, and the significant fall in storm turbidity suggests that sediment delivery
   158	did decline. The invertebrate response appeared sooner than the literature led us to expect,
   159	although only at the wider buffers.
   160	For catchment managers, the most practical finding concerns width. Buffers of 20 metres or
   161	more achieved nearly three times the nitrate reduction of the 10- and 12-metre buffers, and
   162	only the wider buffers improved invertebrate scores. Because farmers chose the width, the
   163	wider buffers may also sit on land with different drainage, so this pattern should be
   164	confirmed before it is used to set a minimum width.
   165	6 Limitations
   166	The study has several limitations. Reaches were not randomly assigned to restoration: they
   167	were chosen where farmers volunteered land, and restored and control reaches may differ in
   168	ways the matching did not capture. With six reaches per group, the study had limited power
   169	to detect moderate effects, which matters for the phosphorus result. Monthly spot sampling
   170	under-represents storm flows, when most phosphorus and sediment are transported. Three
   171	post-planting years are too few to capture the full effect of canopy closure. Finally, the
   172	study did not survey fish, measure groundwater, or record changes in fertiliser use on the
   173	surrounding farms.
   174	7 Conclusions and recommendations
   175	Native woodland buffers combined with livestock exclusion reduced nitrate in Halden
   176	tributaries within three years, and buffers at least 20 metres wide performed best. We
   177	recommend that the Partnership widen the two narrow buffers to at least 20 metres, continue
   178	monitoring until 2027 to capture the effect of canopy closure, and add storm-event
   179	phosphorus sampling at all restored reaches.
results.answer:
The Halden buffers may have reduced phosphorus, but the evidence is not conclusive.

The report says total phosphorus "fell by 19% at restored reaches, from 0.118 to 0.096 mg/L," but the difference was "not statistically significant (p = 0.21)," and the discussion says, "The phosphorus results are less conclusive."

ANSWER: They appeared to bring phosphorus down somewhat, but the report says the result was not statistically significant, so it’s inconclusive.

     2	Final monitoring report, 2021 to 2024. Prepared by the monitoring team of the Halden Vale
     3	Rivers Trust for the Halden Catchment Partnership. Report HVRT-MR-25-02, March 2025.
     4	Reviewed by the Partnership's technical group in February 2025. Distribution: Partnership
     5	members, participating landowners and the regulator's catchment team.
     6	Abstract
     7	Diffuse pollution from livestock farming is the main pressure on the tributaries of the
     8	River Halden. Between January and March 2022 the Halden Catchment Partnership fenced cattle
     9	and sheep out of six tributary reaches and planted native broadleaf woodland buffers 10 to
    10	30 metres wide along both banks. We sampled these six restored reaches and six matched
    11	control reaches every month from January 2021 to December 2024 in a
    12	before-after-control-impact (BACI) design, comparing the 2021 baseline year with 2024, the
    13	third growing season after planting. Mean nitrate-N concentrations at restored reaches fell
    14	by 31% between 2021 and 2024, while concentrations at control reaches changed little. Total
    15	phosphorus and storm-event turbidity also declined at restored reaches, and the mean
    16	macroinvertebrate community index rose by 0.7 points. Responses were strongest where buffers
    17	were at least 20 metres wide. We conclude that woodland buffers of this width are an
    18	effective way to reduce nitrate in lowland livestock catchments, and we recommend widening
    19	buffers narrower than 20 metres where land can be secured.
    20	Keywords: riparian buffer; diffuse pollution; nitrate; phosphorus; turbidity; stream
    21	temperature; macroinvertebrates; BACI design.
    22	
    23	1 Introduction
    24	The River Halden drains about 21,000 hectares of lowland farmland, roughly two thirds of it
    25	grazed grassland. Its tributaries have failed their nutrient standards in every
    26	classification since 2015, mainly because nitrate and phosphorus are washed from fields and
    27	released where livestock have direct access to the channel. Riparian buffers, strips of
    28	permanent vegetation between farmland and the stream, are widely promoted as a low-cost
    29	remedy because they intercept runoff, take up nutrients, stabilise banks and shade the
    30	water. Their performance in practice varies a great deal, however, and few schemes have been
    31	monitored for long enough, or against suitable controls, to separate the effect of the
    32	buffer from changes in weather and farming.
    33	In 2021 the Partnership agreed to fund buffer planting on six tributary reaches and asked
    34	the Trust to find out whether water quality and stream ecology improved as a result. This
    35	report presents the full four years of monitoring. It addresses three questions: whether
    36	nutrient concentrations and turbidity fell at restored reaches relative to controls; whether
    37	conditions for stream invertebrates improved; and whether the response depended on the width
    38	of the buffer.
    39	2 Previous studies
    40	Published evaluations report a wide range of outcomes. In a review of 38 buffer schemes in
    41	temperate Europe, Ostrander and Vey (2018) found a median nitrate reduction of 33% in
    42	shallow groundwater beneath buffers but only 12% in the receiving streams. On the Kell
    43	Water, nitrate-N fell from 6.1 to 4.9 mg/L in the ten years after a 15-metre grass buffer
    44	was established, a reduction of 20%, with no change in total phosphorus (Brennan and
    45	colleagues, 2017). Wooded buffers in the Ardle uplands, by contrast, reduced total
    46	phosphorus by 27% within three years (Haldane and Pike, 2020).
    47	Shading effects are better established. Summer maximum water temperatures beneath a mature
    48	riparian canopy are typically 2 to 4 °C lower than in open reaches (Maddox, 2015), and newly
    49	planted buffers have lowered summer maxima by 0.8 °C within five years (Ferrar and Quine,
    50	2021). Invertebrate responses tend to lag behind chemical change: Ostrander and Vey (2018)
    51	reported that community index scores rose by 0.4 points on average, and only in schemes more
    52	than five years old. Several authors conclude that buffers narrower than 10 metres deliver
    53	little benefit for nitrate (Brennan and colleagues, 2017; Okoro, 2019).
    54	
    55	3 Methods
    56	3.1 Study reaches
    57	Twelve reaches, each 500 metres long, were selected on eight first- and second-order
    58	tributaries. Six were restored and six served as controls. Control reaches were matched to
    59	restored reaches on upstream catchment area, share of grazed grassland and baseline nitrate
    60	concentration, and none was fenced or planted during the study. At restored reaches,
    61	livestock were excluded with post-and-wire fencing, and the strip between the fence and the
    62	bank top was planted at 2,500 trees per hectare with alder, willow, hawthorn and oak. Buffer
    63	width, measured from bank top to fence, ranged from 10 to 30 metres and was set by the
    64	amount of land each farmer was willing to release (Table 1).

    70	3.2 Sampling and laboratory analysis
    71	Spot water samples were taken monthly at the downstream end of every reach, giving 48
    72	sampling occasions per reach over the four years. Automatic samplers collected additional
    73	samples during up to six storm events per reach each year. Nitrate-N and total phosphorus
    74	were analysed by the Trust's accredited laboratory, and turbidity was measured in the field
    75	with a calibrated probe. Duplicate samples and field blanks were analysed with every batch,
    76	and all batches met the laboratory's acceptance criteria. Temperature loggers recorded water
    77	temperature every 15 minutes from May to September. Macroinvertebrates were sampled each
    78	October with a three-minute kick sample and scored on the community index used by the
    79	regional regulator, on which higher scores indicate cleaner water.
    80	3.3 Statistical analysis
    81	The baseline year (2021) was compared with the third year after planting (2024). Annual
    82	means for each reach were analysed with a linear mixed model with reach as a random effect
    83	and period (before or after), group (restored or control) and their interaction as fixed
    84	effects. The interaction term is the BACI effect: the change at restored reaches over and
    85	above the change at control reaches. Group means are reported with the p-value for the
    86	interaction, and p < 0.05 was taken as significant. Because only two restored reaches had
    87	buffers narrower than 20 metres, the comparison between wide and narrow buffers is
    88	descriptive.

   156	sediment and moves during storms, so annual means of monthly spot samples are a noisy

   159	although only at the wider buffers.

   161	more achieved nearly three times the nitrate reduction of the 10- and 12-metre buffers, and

trace.name: lasso
trace.args: {"ask":["the study or report about Halden buffers and phosphorus levels: relevant passages stating whether phosphorus levels went down or not","any results or conclusions about phosphorus levels in Halden buffers"],"budget":5}

results.answer:
Yes, but only weakly.

The report says total phosphorus at restored reaches fell from 0.118 to 0.096 mg/L, a 19% drop, compared with a 10% fall at control reaches. However, the difference was **not statistically significant** (p = 0.21), and the report concludes that “the phosphorus results are less conclusive.”

ANSWER: The Halden buffers were associated with lower phosphorus levels, but the reduction was not statistically significant, so the evidence that they brought phosphorus down is inconclusive.

Summer water temperatures fell at the restored Halden streams after the trees went in. The report says mean summer maximum water temperature at restored reaches dropped from 19.8 °C in 2021 to 18.1 °C in 2024, while control reaches went from 19.6 °C to 19.9 °C.

    27	released where livestock have direct access to the channel. Riparian buffers, strips of

results.answer:
Yes — there is a sign of improvement for the small stream creatures, but it was not universal.

The report says the mean macroinvertebrate community index at restored reaches rose from "4.9 in October 2021 to 5.6 in October 2024," while control reaches only moved from "5.0 to 5.1." So the restored streams did seem to become better places for these small creatures, especially where the buffers were wider, but the narrower-buffer reaches did not show improvement.

  p.1 Evaluation of the Northfold Community Pharmacy Stop-Smoking Programme
  p.1 Twelve-month results of a cluster-randomised trial. Final report to Northfold Council Public Health, November 2024. Prepared by the Northfold Health Services Evaluation Unit.
  p.1 Background: Most smokers who try to stop do so without professional help, and specialist stop-smoking clinics reach few of them. Community pharmacies are open long hours and are visited by many smokers, which makes them a promising place to offer structured support.
  p.1 Methods: Twenty-four community pharmacies were randomly allocated to deliver the programme (12 pharmacies) or usual care (12 pharmacies). The programme offered six weekly one-to-one sessions with a trained pharmacy adviser and up to 12 weeks of free varenicline or combination nicotine replacement therapy. Usual care consisted of brief advice and a referral to the council's telephone quitline. The primary outcome was continuous abstinence from smoking at 52 weeks, confirmed by an exhaled carbon monoxide reading below 10 parts per million.
  p.1 Results: Between March 2022 and February 2023, 2,310 adult smokers enrolled, 1,212 at programme pharmacies and 1,098 at usual-care pharmacies. At 52 weeks, 14.2% of programme participants and 8.9% of usual-care participants were abstinent (adjusted odds ratio 1.71, 95% confidence interval 1.26 to 2.32). The programme also increased validated abstinence at four weeks.
  p.1 Conclusions: Structured support from a trained pharmacy adviser, with free stop-smoking medicine, increased long-term quitting compared with brief advice. Community pharmacies are a practical setting for stop-smoking support in Northfold.
  p.2 About 17% of adults in Northfold smoke, above the regional average, and smoking remains the largest single cause of the gap in life expectancy between the most and least deprived parts of the district. The council's specialist stop-smoking clinic sees around 600 smokers a year, a small fraction of those who try to quit. In 2021 the council commissioned a pharmacy-based programme to reach more smokers and asked the Evaluation Unit to test it against usual care before deciding whether to extend it across the district.
  p.2 Evidence on pharmacy-delivered support is mixed. A national audit of pharmacy stop-smoking services found an average four-week quit rate of 35%, although fewer than half of the reported quits were confirmed by carbon monoxide testing (Lomax, 2019). In a cluster trial in 16 pharmacies in Tayford, Ridley and colleagues (2020) reported continuous abstinence at 52 weeks of 11.5% with behavioural support plus nicotine replacement therapy, against 7.2% with brief advice.

results.answer:
The main results were:

- The trial enrolled 2,310 adult smokers across 24 pharmacies.
- At 52 weeks, **14.2%** of participants in the pharmacy programme were abstinent, compared with **8.9%** in usual care.
- This corresponded to an **adjusted odds ratio of 1.71** with a **95% confidence interval of 1.26 to 2.32**.
- The programme also increased **validated abstinence at four weeks**.

Overall, the report concluded that structured support from a trained pharmacy adviser, plus free stop-smoking medicine, **increased long-term quitting compared with brief advice**.

ANSWER: The Northfold pharmacy stop-smoking trial found that the pharmacy programme improved quit rates: 14.2% abstinent at 52 weeks versus 8.9% with usual care, with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.71 (95% CI 1.26 to 2.32), and it also increased validated four-week abstinence.

The main results in the final evaluation report were:

- **52-week continuous abstinence**: **14.2%** of programme participants vs **8.9%** of usual-care participants, with an **adjusted odds ratio of 1.71 (95% confidence interval 1.26 to 2.32; p < 0.001)**.
- **4-week validated abstinence**: **41.6%** vs **27.3%**.
- **26-week self-reported 7-day abstinence**: **22.4%** vs **15.0%**.
- The programme also reduced cigarettes smoked among continuing smokers: **11.4** per day vs **13.6** per day.
- No serious adverse event was judged to be related to the programme.

    24	1 Background
    25	About 17% of adults in Northfold smoke, above the regional average, and smoking remains the
    26	largest single cause of the gap in life expectancy between the most and least deprived parts
    27	of the district. The council's specialist stop-smoking clinic sees around 600 smokers a
    28	year, a small fraction of those who try to quit. In 2021 the council commissioned a
    29	pharmacy-based programme to reach more smokers and asked the Evaluation Unit to test it
    30	against usual care before deciding whether to extend it across the district.
    31	2 Previous research
    32	Evidence on pharmacy-delivered support is mixed. A national audit of pharmacy stop-smoking
    33	services found an average four-week quit rate of 35%, although fewer than half of the
    34	reported quits were confirmed by carbon monoxide testing (Lomax, 2019). In a cluster trial
    35	in 16 pharmacies in Tayford, Ridley and colleagues (2020) reported continuous abstinence at
    36	52 weeks of 11.5% with behavioural support plus nicotine replacement therapy, against 7.2%
    37	with brief advice.
    38	Medication choice matters. In specialist clinics, varenicline has produced 52-week
    39	continuous abstinence of around 23%, compared with 16% for combination nicotine replacement
    40	(Ashworth and Nair, 2016). Results for heavier smokers are less consistent: one trial found
    41	that smokers of 20 or more cigarettes a day were half as likely as lighter smokers to remain
    42	abstinent at 52 weeks (Kerr, 2018), while another found no difference by smoking level
    43	(Duval and Haas, 2021). Few trials have reported results separately for older smokers.
    44	
    45	3 Methods
    46	3.1 Design and setting
    47	This was a pragmatic cluster-randomised trial. All 41 community pharmacies in Northfold were
    48	invited, and 24 agreed to take part. Pharmacies were randomised in pairs matched on monthly
    49	prescription volume and local deprivation, with 12 allocated to the programme and 12 to
    50	usual care. Randomisation was carried out by a statistician who had no contact with the
    51	pharmacies.
    52	3.2 Participants
    53	Pharmacy staff invited customers who smoked to take part. Adults aged 18 or over who smoked
    54	at least five cigarettes a day and wanted to stop within the next month were eligible.
    55	Pregnant women were not eligible, because they are referred to the specialist maternity
    56	stop-smoking service, and people already using a stop-smoking medicine were also excluded.
    57	3.3 Programme and usual care
    58	In programme pharmacies, a trained adviser offered six weekly one-to-one sessions of about
    59	20 minutes, starting one week before the quit date. Advisers were pharmacy staff who had
    60	completed a two-day accredited training course. Participants chose either varenicline or
    61	combination nicotine replacement therapy (a patch plus a short-acting product), supplied
    62	free for up to 12 weeks. In usual-care pharmacies, staff gave brief advice and a written
    63	referral to the council's telephone quitline, and customers could buy nicotine replacement
    64	products as normal.
    65	3.4 Outcomes and analysis
    66	The primary outcome was self-reported continuous abstinence from two weeks after the quit
    67	date to 52 weeks, allowing no more than five cigarettes in total, confirmed by an exhaled
    68	carbon monoxide reading below 10 parts per million. Secondary outcomes were carbon
    69	monoxide-validated abstinence at four weeks and self-reported seven-day abstinence at 26
    70	weeks. Participants lost to follow-up were counted as smokers. Groups were compared with
    71	logistic regression adjusted for pharmacy pair, age, sex and cigarettes per day, with
    72	standard errors allowing for clustering by pharmacy. Subgroup analyses by cigarettes per day
    73	(fewer than 20, or 20 or more) and by sex were specified in advance.
    74	
    75	4 Results
    76	4.1 Participants
    77	Between March 2022 and February 2023, 2,310 smokers enrolled: 1,212 at programme pharmacies
    78	and 1,098 at usual-care pharmacies. The two groups were similar at enrolment (Table 1).
    79	Participants had a mean age of 44 years, 52% were women, and they smoked a mean of 17
    80	cigarettes a day. Programme pharmacies enrolled a median of 98 participants each and
    81	usual-care pharmacies a median of 89. Follow-up at 52 weeks was completed by 78% of
    82	programme participants and 73% of usual-care participants.

    92	At 52 weeks, 172 of 1,212 programme participants (14.2%) were continuously abstinent with
    93	carbon monoxide confirmation, compared with 98 of 1,098 usual-care participants (8.9%). The
    94	adjusted odds ratio was 1.71 (95% confidence interval 1.26 to 2.32; p < 0.001), and the
    95	absolute difference was 5.3 percentage points. Sensitivity analyses using multiple
    96	imputation for missing follow-up gave similar results.
    97	
    98	4.3 Secondary outcomes
    99	At four weeks after the quit date, 41.6% of programme participants were abstinent with
   100	carbon monoxide confirmation, compared with 27.3% in usual care. At 26 weeks, 22.4% of
   101	programme participants and 15.0% of usual-care participants reported that they had not
   102	smoked in the previous seven days. These 26-week figures are self-reported, as carbon

   113	least four. Of the 1,212 programme participants, 58% chose varenicline and 42% chose

   115	those who chose varenicline and 11.6% among those who chose nicotine replacement, although

   120	Among participants who smoked 20 or more cigarettes a day at enrolment (n = 740), 52-week
   121	validated abstinence was 10.3% with the programme and 8.1% with usual care. However, this
   122	difference was not statistically significant (adjusted odds ratio 1.29, 95% confidence
   123	interval 0.78 to 2.14). Among those who smoked fewer than 20 cigarettes a day, abstinence
   124	was 16.2% with the programme and 9.3% with usual care. The test for interaction between
   125	trial group and smoking level was not significant (p = 0.18). Results for men and women were
   126	similar.

   128	were abstinent at 52 weeks with the programme compared with 9.6% in usual care. Older
   129	participants were also more likely to attend at least four sessions (74%, against 61% of
   130	those under 60). This age analysis was not specified in advance and should be treated as
   131	exploratory.

   133	Nausea was the most common adverse event, reported by 18% of participants who used
   134	varenicline and 6% of those who used nicotine replacement therapy. Sleep disturbance was
   135	reported by 9% of programme participants. No serious adverse event was judged to be related
   136	to the programme.

   139	The programme increased carbon monoxide-validated continuous abstinence at 52 weeks by 5.3
   140	percentage points, a relative increase of about 60% over usual care. This is a larger effect
   141	than in the Tayford trial reviewed in Section 2, which may reflect the free choice of
   142	varenicline and the requirement that advisers complete accredited training. The four-week
   143	quit rate was well above usual care but below the average reported by the national audit,
   144	which counted unconfirmed quits.
   145	The benefit appeared to be concentrated among lighter smokers. Smokers of 20 or more
   146	cigarettes a day gained little from the programme as delivered, which suggests that they may
   147	need higher-dose nicotine replacement or longer support. The apparent benefit for
   148	participants aged 60 and over is encouraging, but it comes from an unplanned analysis and
   149	needs confirmation.

   151	rate seen in the trial, it would reach around 4,000 smokers a year, several times the number
   152	seen by the specialist clinic. At the effect observed in the trial, that would mean roughly
   153	200 more people a year still not smoking after twelve months than with usual care.

   155	Pharmacies volunteered to take part, and the 24 trial pharmacies may be more motivated than

   157	outcome was biochemically confirmed. Follow-up at 52 weeks was lower in the usual-care

    35	in 16 pharmacies in Tayford, Ridley and colleagues (2020) reported continuous abstinence at
    36	52 weeks of 11.5% with behavioural support plus nicotine replacement therapy, against 7.2%
    37	with brief advice.
    38	Medication choice matters. In specialist clinics, varenicline has produced 52-week
    39	continuous abstinence of around 23%, compared with 16% for combination nicotine replacement
    40	(Ashworth and Nair, 2016). Results for heavier smokers are less consistent: one trial found
    41	that smokers of 20 or more cigarettes a day were half as likely as lighter smokers to remain
    42	abstinent at 52 weeks (Kerr, 2018), while another found no difference by smoking level
    43	(Duval and Haas, 2021). Few trials have reported results separately for older smokers.
    44	
    45	3 Methods
    46	3.1 Design and setting
    47	This was a pragmatic cluster-randomised trial. All 41 community pharmacies in Northfold were
    48	invited, and 24 agreed to take part. Pharmacies were randomised in pairs matched on monthly
    49	prescription volume and local deprivation, with 12 allocated to the programme and 12 to
    50	usual care. Randomisation was carried out by a statistician who had no contact with the
    51	pharmacies.
    52	3.2 Participants
    53	Pharmacy staff invited customers who smoked to take part. Adults aged 18 or over who smoked
    54	at least five cigarettes a day and wanted to stop within the next month were eligible.
    55	Pregnant women were not eligible, because they are referred to the specialist maternity
    56	stop-smoking service, and people already using a stop-smoking medicine were also excluded.
    57	3.3 Programme and usual care
    58	In programme pharmacies, a trained adviser offered six weekly one-to-one sessions of about
    59	20 minutes, starting one week before the quit date. Advisers were pharmacy staff who had
    60	completed a two-day accredited training course. Participants chose either varenicline or
    61	combination nicotine replacement therapy (a patch plus a short-acting product), supplied
    62	free for up to 12 weeks. In usual-care pharmacies, staff gave brief advice and a written
    63	referral to the council's telephone quitline, and customers could buy nicotine replacement
    64	products as normal.
    65	3.4 Outcomes and analysis
    66	The primary outcome was self-reported continuous abstinence from two weeks after the quit
    67	date to 52 weeks, allowing no more than five cigarettes in total, confirmed by an exhaled
    68	carbon monoxide reading below 10 parts per million. Secondary outcomes were carbon
    69	monoxide-validated abstinence at four weeks and self-reported seven-day abstinence at 26
    70	weeks. Participants lost to follow-up were counted as smokers. Groups were compared with
    71	logistic regression adjusted for pharmacy pair, age, sex and cigarettes per day, with
    72	standard errors allowing for clustering by pharmacy. Subgroup analyses by cigarettes per day
    73	(fewer than 20, or 20 or more) and by sex were specified in advance.
    74	
    75	4 Results
    76	4.1 Participants
    77	Between March 2022 and February 2023, 2,310 smokers enrolled: 1,212 at programme pharmacies
    78	and 1,098 at usual-care pharmacies. The two groups were similar at enrolment (Table 1).
    79	Participants had a mean age of 44 years, 52% were women, and they smoked a mean of 17
    80	cigarettes a day. Programme pharmacies enrolled a median of 98 participants each and
    81	usual-care pharmacies a median of 89. Follow-up at 52 weeks was completed by 78% of
    82	programme participants and 73% of usual-care participants.

    90	36
    91	4.2 Primary outcome
    92	At 52 weeks, 172 of 1,212 programme participants (14.2%) were continuously abstinent with
    93	carbon monoxide confirmation, compared with 98 of 1,098 usual-care participants (8.9%). The
    94	adjusted odds ratio was 1.71 (95% confidence interval 1.26 to 2.32; p < 0.001), and the
    95	absolute difference was 5.3 percentage points. Sensitivity analyses using multiple
    96	imputation for missing follow-up gave similar results.
    97	
    98	4.3 Secondary outcomes
    99	At four weeks after the quit date, 41.6% of programme participants were abstinent with
   100	carbon monoxide confirmation, compared with 27.3% in usual care. At 26 weeks, 22.4% of
   101	programme participants and 15.0% of usual-care participants reported that they had not
   102	smoked in the previous seven days. These 26-week figures are self-reported, as carbon
   103	monoxide was not measured at that point. All outcomes, including the amount smoked by
   104	participants who were still smoking at 52 weeks, are shown in Table 2.

   111	4.4 Programme delivery
   112	Programme participants attended a median of five of the six sessions, and 63% attended at
   113	least four. Of the 1,212 programme participants, 58% chose varenicline and 42% chose
   114	combination nicotine replacement therapy. At 52 weeks, validated abstinence was 16.1% among
   115	those who chose varenicline and 11.6% among those who chose nicotine replacement, although
   116	participants were not randomised to medication and these groups differed in age and smoking
   117	level.

   121	validated abstinence was 10.3% with the programme and 8.1% with usual care. However, this
   122	difference was not statistically significant (adjusted odds ratio 1.29, 95% confidence
   123	interval 0.78 to 2.14). Among those who smoked fewer than 20 cigarettes a day, abstinence
   124	was 16.2% with the programme and 9.3% with usual care. The test for interaction between
   125	trial group and smoking level was not significant (p = 0.18). Results for men and women were
   126	similar.

   128	were abstinent at 52 weeks with the programme compared with 9.6% in usual care. Older
   129	participants were also more likely to attend at least four sessions (74%, against 61% of
   130	those under 60). This age analysis was not specified in advance and should be treated as
   131	exploratory.

   133	Nausea was the most common adverse event, reported by 18% of participants who used
   134	varenicline and 6% of those who used nicotine replacement therapy. Sleep disturbance was
   135	reported by 9% of programme participants. No serious adverse event was judged to be related
   136	to the programme.

   139	The programme increased carbon monoxide-validated continuous abstinence at 52 weeks by 5.3
   140	percentage points, a relative increase of about 60% over usual care. This is a larger effect
   141	than in the Tayford trial reviewed in Section 2, which may reflect the free choice of
   142	varenicline and the requirement that advisers complete accredited training. The four-week
   143	quit rate was well above usual care but below the average reported by the national audit,
   144	which counted unconfirmed quits.

   146	cigarettes a day gained little from the programme as delivered, which suggests that they may
   147	need higher-dose nicotine replacement or longer support. The apparent benefit for
   148	participants aged 60 and over is encouraging, but it comes from an unplanned analysis and
   149	needs confirmation.

   151	rate seen in the trial, it would reach around 4,000 smokers a year, several times the number

I found two different “one-year” figures in the files:

- The final trial report says: “At 52 weeks, 172 of 1,212 programme participants (14.2%) were continuously abstinent with carbon monoxide confirmation…”
- The briefing memo says: “At 12 months, 16.4% of programme participants were still not smoking, confirmed by a carbon monoxide breath test…”

These don’t match. Which source should I use for the press release: the final evaluation report’s 14.2%, or the briefing memo’s 16.4%?

ANSWER: There are conflicting one-year quit rates in the files: 14.2% in the final report and 16.4% in the briefing memo. Please confirm which one you want used.

The files give two different one-year figures, so I can’t choose between them from the material provided:

- The final report says that at 52 weeks, **“14.2% of programme participants”** were abstinent, and this was **“Validated continuous abstinence at 52 weeks (%)”**.
- The briefing memo says that at 12 months, **“16.4% of programme participants were still not smoking”**, confirmed by a carbon monoxide breath test.

So the report and memo do not match on the one-year quit rate. If this is for a press release, you should first confirm which figure the director wants used.  
ANSWER: The files conflict: the report gives **14.2%** at 52 weeks, while the memo gives **16.4%** at 12 months.

     5	Purpose
     6	
     7	This memo summarises the final evaluation report on the community pharmacy stop-smoking programme and asks you to approve extending the programme to all pharmacies in Northfold from April 2025.
     8	
     9	Background
    10	
    11	The programme was tested in a cluster-randomised trial in which 12 pharmacies delivered it and 12 provided usual care, meaning brief advice and a referral to the telephone quitline.     14	
    15	The programme substantially increased short-term quitting. Four weeks after their quit date, 41.6% of programme participants had stopped smoking, confirmed by a breath test, against 27.3% in usual care.
    16	
    17	The longer-term result is the one that matters most. At 12 months, 16.4% of programme participants were still not smoking, confirmed by a carbon monoxide breath test, compared with 8.9% of those who received usual care. The evaluation team's adjusted odds ratio for this comparison was 1.71.
    18	
    19	Smokers aged 60 and over did especially well, with around one in five still smoke-free at 12 months. Nearly two thirds of participants (63%) attended at least four of the six sessions, and no serious side effects were linked to the programme.
    20	
    21	The programme also reached the people we most need to reach: 38% of programme participants lived in the most deprived fifth of areas in the district.
    22	
    23	Recommendation
    24	
    25	Approve extension of the programme to all 41 community pharmacies in Northfold from April 2025. The 17 pharmacies that did not take part in the trial will need their staff trained before then, and the two-day adviser course can be run in February and March 2025.
    26	
    27	Risks
    28	
    29	Demand for adviser time may exceed capacity in the busiest town-centre pharmacies. Supply arrangements for varenicline need to be confirmed with the local pharmaceutical committee. results.answer:
The report does not show a clear, statistically significant benefit for pack-a-day smokers.

In the subgroup of participants who smoked **20 or more cigarettes a day**:
- **10.3%** in the programme group were abstinent at 52 weeks
- **8.1%** in usual care were abstinent
- the adjusted odds ratio was **1.29 (95% CI 0.78 to 2.14)**

The report says this difference **was not statistically significant**, and the discussion notes that **“Smokers of 20 or more cigarettes a day gained little from the programme as delivered”** and may need additional support.

ANSWER: The programme did not clearly help pack-a-day smokers; their quit rate was slightly higher, but the difference was not statistically significant and the report says they gained little from the programme as delivered.

     6	
     7	This memo summarises the final evaluation report on the community pharmacy stop-smoking programme and asks you to approve extending the programme to all pharmacies in Northfold from April 2025.
     8	
     9	Background
    10	
    11	The programme was tested in a cluster-randomised trial in which 12 pharmacies delivered it and 12 provided usual care, meaning brief advice and a referral to the telephone quitline.     14	
    15	The programme substantially increased short-term quitting. Four weeks after their quit date, 41.6% of programme participants had stopped smoking, confirmed by a breath test, against 27.3% in usual care.
    16	
    17	The longer-term result is the one that matters most. At 12 months, 16.4% of programme participants were still not smoking, confirmed by a carbon monoxide breath test, compared with 8.9% of those who received usual care. The evaluation team's adjusted odds ratio for this comparison was 1.71.
    18	
    19	Smokers aged 60 and over did especially well, with around one in five still smoke-free at 12 months. Nearly two thirds of participants (63%) attended at least four of the six sessions, and no serious side effects were linked to the programme.
    20

    22

    24	
    25	Approve extension of the programme to all 41 community pharmacies in Northfold from April 2025. The 17 pharmacies that did not take part in the trial will need their staff trained before then, and the two-day adviser course can be run in February and March 2025.
    26	
    27	Risks
    28	
    29	Demand for adviser time may exceed capacity in the busiest town-centre pharmacies. Supply arrangements for varenicline need to be confirmed with the local pharmaceutical committee.    128	were abstinent at 52 weeks with the programme compared with 9.6% in usual care. Older
   129	participants were also more likely to attend at least four sessions (74%, against 61% of
   130	those under 60). This age analysis was not specified in advance and should be treated as
   131	exploratory.
   132	4.6 Adverse events
   133	Nausea was the most common adverse event, reported by 18% of participants who used
   134	varenicline and 6% of those who used nicotine replacement therapy. Sleep disturbance was
   135	reported by 9% of programme participants. No serious adverse event was judged to be related
   136	to the programme.
   137	
   138	5 Discussion
   139	The programme increased carbon monoxide-validated continuous abstinence at 52 weeks by 5.3
   140	percentage points, a relative increase of about 60% over usual care. This is a larger effect
   141	than in the Tayford trial reviewed in Section 2, which may reflect the free choice of
   142	varenicline and the requirement that advisers complete accredited training. The four-week
   143	quit rate was well above usual care but below the average reported by the national audit,
   144	which counted unconfirmed quits.
   145	The benefit appeared to be concentrated among lighter smokers. Smokers of 20 or more
   146	cigarettes a day gained little from the programme as delivered, which suggests that they may
   147	need higher-dose nicotine replacement or longer support. The apparent benefit for
   148	participants aged 60 and over is encouraging, but it comes from an unplanned analysis and
   149	needs confirmation.
   150	If the programme were extended to all 41 pharmacies in Northfold and enrolled smokers at the
   151	rate seen in the trial, it would reach around 4,000 smokers a year, several times the number
   152	seen by the specialist clinic. At the effect observed in the trial, that would mean roughly
   153	200 more people a year still not smoking after twelve months than with usual care.
   154	6 Limitations
   155	Pharmacies volunteered to take part, and the 24 trial pharmacies may be more motivated than
   156	the 17 that declined. Participants and advisers knew their allocation, although the primary
   157	outcome was biochemically confirmed. Follow-up at 52 weeks was lower in the usual-care
   158	group, and counting those lost to follow-up as smokers may slightly favour the programme.
   159	The trial did not collect data on e-cigarette use, which was common during the study period,
   160	and it was not designed to assess costs.
   161	
   162	7 Conclusions
   163	Structured support from trained pharmacy advisers, with free stop-smoking medicine,
   164	increased long-term quitting compared with brief advice and referral. The council should
   165	consider extending the programme to all pharmacies in Northfold, with additional support for
   166	heavy smokers, and should monitor quit rates in routine delivery.

results.answer:
In practice, the programme kept people engaged fairly well: participants attended a median of five of the six sessions, and 63% attended at least four.

For medicines, 58% chose varenicline and 42% chose combination nicotine replacement therapy.

Side effects were mostly mild: nausea was the most common, reported by 18% of varenicline users and 6% of nicotine replacement users. Sleep disturbance was reported by 9% of programme participants. No serious adverse event was judged to be related to the programme.

ANSWER: People mostly kept coming, with a median of five sessions attended and 63% attending at least four of six. They chose either varenicline (58%) or combination nicotine replacement therapy (42%). Side effects were mainly nausea and some sleep disturbance, and no serious side effects were linked to the programme.

     1	Evaluation of the Northfold Community Pharmacy Stop-Smoking Programme
     2	Twelve-month results of a cluster-randomised trial. Final report to Northfold Council Public
     3	Health, November 2024. Prepared by the Northfold Health Services Evaluation Unit.
     4	Abstract
     5	Background: Most smokers who try to stop do so without professional help, and specialist
     6	stop-smoking clinics reach few of them. Community pharmacies are open long hours and are
     7	visited by many smokers, which makes them a promising place to offer structured support.
     8	Methods: Twenty-four community pharmacies were randomly allocated to deliver the programme
     9	(12 pharmacies) or usual care (12 pharmacies). The programme offered six weekly one-to-one
    10	sessions with a trained pharmacy adviser and up to 12 weeks of free varenicline or
    11	combination nicotine replacement therapy. Usual care consisted of brief advice and a
    12	referral to the council's telephone quitline. The primary outcome was continuous abstinence
    13	from smoking at 52 weeks, confirmed by an exhaled carbon monoxide reading below 10 parts per
    14	million.
    15	Results: Between March 2022 and February 2023, 2,310 adult smokers enrolled, 1,212 at
    16	programme pharmacies and 1,098 at usual-care pharmacies. At 52 weeks, 14.2% of programme
    17	participants and 8.9% of usual-care participants were abstinent (adjusted odds ratio 1.71,
    18	95% confidence interval 1.26 to 2.32). The programme also increased validated abstinence at
    19	four weeks.
    20	Conclusions: Structured support from a trained pharmacy adviser, with free stop-smoking
    21	medicine, increased long-term quitting compared with brief advice. Community pharmacies are
    22	a practical setting for stop-smoking support in Northfold.
    23	
    24	1 Background
    25	About 17% of adults in Northfold smoke, above the regional average, and smoking remains the
    26	largest single cause of the gap in life expectancy between the most and least deprived parts
    27	of the district. The council's specialist stop-smoking clinic sees around 600 smokers a
    28	year, a small fraction of those who try to quit. In 2021 the council commissioned a
    29	pharmacy-based programme to reach more smokers and asked the Evaluation Unit to test it
    30	against usual care before deciding whether to extend it across the district.
    31	2 Previous research
    32	Evidence on pharmacy-delivered support is mixed. A national audit of pharmacy stop-smoking
    33	services found an average four-week quit rate of 35%, although fewer than half of the
    34	reported quits were confirmed by carbon monoxide testing (Lomax, 2019). In a cluster trial
    35	in 16 pharmacies in Tayford, Ridley and colleagues (2020) reported continuous abstinence at
    36	52 weeks of 11.5% with behavioural support plus nicotine replacement therapy, against 7.2%
    37	with brief advice.
    38	Medication choice matters. In specialist clinics, varenicline has produced 52-week
    39	continuous abstinence of around 23%, compared with 16% for combination nicotine replacement
    40	(Ashworth and Nair, 2016). Results for heavier smokers are less consistent: one trial found
    41	that smokers of 20 or more cigarettes a day were half as likely as lighter smokers to remain
    42	abstinent at 52 weeks (Kerr, 2018), while another found no difference by smoking level
    43	(Duval and Haas, 2021). Few trials have reported results separately for older smokers.
    44	
    45	3 Methods
    46	3.1 Design and setting
    47	This was a pragmatic cluster-randomised trial. All 41 community pharmacies in Northfold were
    48	invited, and 24 agreed to take part. Pharmacies were randomised in pairs matched on monthly
    49	prescription volume and local deprivation, with 12 allocated to the programme and 12 to
    50	usual care. Randomisation was carried out by a statistician who had no contact with the
    51	pharmacies.
    52	3.2 Participants
    53	Pharmacy staff invited customers who smoked to take part. Adults aged 18 or over who smoked
    54	at least five cigarettes a day and wanted to stop within the next month were eligible.
    55	Pregnant women were not eligible, because they are referred to the specialist maternity
    56	stop-smoking service, and people already using a stop-smoking medicine were also excluded.
    57	3.3 Programme and usual care
    58	In programme pharmacies, a trained adviser offered six weekly one-to-one sessions of about
    59	20 minutes, starting one week before the quit date. Advisers were pharmacy staff who had
    60	completed a two-day accredited training course. Participants chose either varenicline or
    61	combination nicotine replacement therapy (a patch plus a short-acting product), supplied
    62	free for up to 12 weeks. In usual-care pharmacies, staff gave brief advice and a written
    63	referral to the council's telephone quitline, and customers could buy nicotine replacement
    64	products as normal.
    65	3.4 Outcomes and analysis
    66	The primary outcome was self-reported continuous abstinence from two weeks after the quit
    67	date to 52 weeks, allowing no more than five cigarettes in total, confirmed by an exhaled
    68	carbon monoxide reading below 10 parts per million. Secondary outcomes were carbon
    69	monoxide-validated abstinence at four weeks and self-reported seven-day abstinence at 26
    70	weeks. Participants lost to follow-up were counted as smokers. Groups were compared with
    71	logistic regression adjusted for pharmacy pair, age, sex and cigarettes per day, with
    72	standard errors allowing for clustering by pharmacy. Subgroup analyses by cigarettes per day
    73	(fewer than 20, or 20 or more) and by sex were specified in advance.
    74	
    75	4 Results
    76	4.1 Participants
    77	Between March 2022 and February 2023, 2,310 smokers enrolled: 1,212 at programme pharmacies
    78	and 1,098 at usual-care pharmacies. The two groups were similar at enrolment (Table 1).
    79	Participants had a mean age of 44 years, 52% were women, and they smoked a mean of 17
    80	cigarettes a day. Programme pharmacies enrolled a median of 98 participants each and
    81	usual-care pharmacies a median of 89. Follow-up at 52 weeks was completed by 78% of
    82	programme participants and 73% of usual-care participants.

    91	4.2 Primary outcome
    92	At 52 weeks, 172 of 1,212 programme participants (14.2%) were continuously abstinent with
    93	carbon monoxide confirmation, compared with 98 of 1,098 usual-care participants (8.9%). The
    94	adjusted odds ratio was 1.71 (95% confidence interval 1.26 to 2.32; p < 0.001), and the

    96	imputation for missing follow-up gave similar results.

    98	4.3 Secondary outcomes
    99	At four weeks after the quit date, 41.6% of programme participants were abstinent with
   100	carbon monoxide confirmation, compared with 27.3% in usual care. At 26 weeks, 22.4% of
   101	programme participants and 15.0% of usual-care participants reported that they had not
   102	smoked in the previous seven days. These 26-week figures are self-reported, as carbon
   103	monoxide was not measured at that point. All outcomes, including the amount smoked by
   104	participants who were still smoking at 52 weeks, are shown in Table 2.
   105	Table 2. Primary and secondary outcomes by trial group.
   106	Outcome Programme Usual care Adjusted odds ratio (95% CI)
   107	Validated abstinence at 4 weeks (%) 41.6 27.3 1.92 (1.55 to 2.38)
   108	Self-reported 7-day abstinence at 26 weeks (%) 22.4 15.0 1.63 (1.29 to 2.06)
   109	Validated continuous abstinence at 52 weeks (%) 14.2 8.9 1.71 (1.26 to 2.32)
   110	Cigarettes per day at 52 weeks among continuing smokers, mean 11.4 13.6 not applicable
   111	4.4 Programme delivery
   112	Programme participants attended a median of five of the six sessions, and 63% attended at
   113	least four. Of the 1,212 programme participants, 58% chose varenicline and 42% chose
   114	combination nicotine replacement therapy. At 52 weeks, validated abstinence was 16.1% among
   115	those who chose varenicline and 11.6% among those who chose nicotine replacement, although
   116	participants were not randomised to medication and these groups differed in age and smoking
   117	level.
   118	
   119	4.5 Subgroup analyses
   120	Among participants who smoked 20 or more cigarettes a day at enrolment (n = 740), 52-week
   121	validated abstinence was 10.3% with the programme and 8.1% with usual care. However, this
   122	difference was not statistically significant (adjusted odds ratio 1.29, 95% confidence
   123	interval 0.78 to 2.14). Among those who smoked fewer than 20 cigarettes a day, abstinence
   124	was 16.2% with the programme and 9.3% with usual care. The test for interaction between
   125	trial group and smoking level was not significant (p = 0.18). Results for men and women were
   126	similar.
   127	The programme's effect appeared larger among participants aged 60 and over, of whom 19.8%
   128	were abstinent at 52 weeks with the programme compared with 9.6% in usual care. Older
   129	participants were also more likely to attend at least four sessions (74%, against 61% of
   130	those under 60). This age analysis was not specified in advance and should be treated as
   131	exploratory.
   132	4.6 Adverse events
   133	Nausea was the most common adverse event, reported by 18% of participants who used
   134	varenicline and 6% of those who used nicotine replacement therapy. Sleep disturbance was
   135	reported by 9% of programme participants. No serious adverse event was judged to be related
   136	to the programme.
   137	
   138	5 Discussion
   139	The programme increased carbon monoxide-validated continuous abstinence at 52 weeks by 5.3
   140	percentage points, a relative increase of about 60% over usual care. This is a larger effect
   141	than in the Tayford trial reviewed in Section 2, which may reflect the free choice of
   142	varenicline and the requirement that advisers complete accredited training. The four-week
   143	quit rate was well above usual care but below the average reported by the national audit,
   144	which counted unconfirmed quits.
   145	The benefit appeared to be concentrated among lighter smokers. Smokers of 20 or more
   146	cigarettes a day gained little from the programme as delivered, which suggests that they may
   147	need higher-dose nicotine replacement or longer support. The apparent benefit for
   148	participants aged 60 and over is encouraging, but it comes from an unplanned analysis and
   149	needs confirmation.
   150	If the programme were extended to all 41 pharmacies in Northfold and enrolled smokers at the
   151	rate seen in the trial, it would reach around 4,000 smokers a year, several times the number
   152	seen by the specialist clinic. At the effect observed in the trial, that would mean roughly
   153	200 more people a year still not smoking after twelve months than with usual care.
   154	6 Limitations
   155	Pharmacies volunteered to take part, and the 24 trial pharmacies may be more motivated than
   156	the 17 that declined. Participants and advisers knew their allocation, although the primary
   157	outcome was biochemically confirmed. Follow-up at 52 weeks was lower in the usual-care
   158	group, and counting those lost to follow-up as smokers may slightly favour the programme.
   159	The trial did not collect data on e-cigarette use, which was common during the study period,
   160	and it was not designed to assess costs.
   161	
   162	7 Conclusions
   163	Structured support from trained pharmacy advisers, with free stop-smoking medicine,
   164	increased long-term quitting compared with brief advice and referral. The council should
   165	consider extending the programme to all pharmacies in Northfold, with additional support for
   166	heavy smokers, and should monitor quit rates in routine delivery.
   167	Acknowledgements
   168	We thank the pharmacists, advisers and customers who took part, the members of the trial
   169	steering committee and the council's tobacco control team. The trial was funded by Northfold
   170	Council Public Health. The authors declare no competing interests.
   171	Abbreviations
   172	CI, confidence interval; CO, carbon monoxide; NRT, nicotine replacement therapy; ppm, parts
   173	per million.
   174	References
   175	Ashworth, J. and Nair, S. (2016). Varenicline and combination nicotine replacement in
   176	specialist stop-smoking clinics: twelve-month outcomes. Addiction Practice 22, 310-318.
   177	Duval, M. and Haas, E. (2021). Smoking level and success in community stop-smoking support.
   178	Cessation Studies Quarterly 9, 55-63.
   179	Kerr, A. (2018). Heavy smokers in stop-smoking trials: a pooled analysis. Cessation Studies
   180	Quarterly 6, 140-149.
   181	Lomax, H. (2019). National audit of pharmacy stop-smoking services. Health Audit Office,
   182	Report 4.
   183	Ridley, F., Osei, K. and Lund, P. (2020). Behavioural support in community pharmacies: a
   184	cluster-randomised trial in Tayford. Pharmacy Practice Research 17, 88-97.

In practice, the programme seemed to run well:

- People did keep coming: participants attended a **median of five of the six sessions**, and **63% attended at least four**.
- Medicine choices were split between the two options offered: **58% chose varenicline** and **42% chose combination nicotine replacement therapy**.
- Side effects were reported, but nothing serious was linked to the programme. The main ones were **nausea** and **sleep disturbance**. Nausea was reported by **18% of varenicline users** and **6% of nicotine replacement users**; **sleep disturbance** was reported by **9% of programme participants** overall. **No serious adverse event was judged to be related to the programme**.

ANSWER: Attendance was good, most people took the sessions regularly; most chose varenicline rather than combination nicotine replacement therapy; and there were some side effects (mainly nausea and sleep disturbance) but no serious programme-related side effects.

In practice, attendance was fairly good:

- Participants attended a **median of five of the six sessions**, and **63% attended at least four**.
- Of the **1,212** programme participants, **58% chose varenicline** and **42% chose combination nicotine replacement therapy**.

Side effects were reported, but no serious programme-related harms were found:

- **Nausea** was reported by **18%** of participants who used varenicline and **6%** of those who used nicotine replacement therapy.
- **Sleep disturbance** was reported by **9%** of programme participants.
- **No serious adverse event was judged to be related to the programme.**

One note: the briefing memo says that at 12 months **“16.4%”** of programme participants were still not smoking, but the final evaluation report says **“14.2%”** at 52 weeks. The files do not explain that discrepancy.

ANSWER: People generally kept coming: they attended a median of five of the six sessions, and 63% attended at least four. Most chose varenicline (58%), with 42% choosing combination nicotine replacement therapy. Side effects were mainly nausea (18% with varenicline, 6% with nicotine replacement therapy) and sleep disturbance (9% overall), and no serious adverse event was judged to be related to the programme.
