     1	School Streets Pilot Evaluation: Traffic, Air Quality and Travel to School
     2	Final report, October 2025. Prepared by the Transport Policy and Research Team, Brackenford
     3	Borough Council, with the Centre for Urban Air Research, University of Westmoor.
     4	Abstract
     5	Background. School Streets are timed road closures that restrict motor traffic on the street
     6	outside a school at the start and end of the school day. Brackenford Borough Council piloted
     7	School Streets at 12 primary schools during the 2024 to 2025 school year.
     8	Methods. We compared the pilot period, January to June 2025, with a baseline period covering
     9	the same months of 2024. Motor traffic was counted by automatic number plate recognition
    10	cameras, nitrogen dioxide (NO2) was measured with diffusion tubes at each school gate and on
    11	nearby boundary roads, and travel to school was recorded in hands-up surveys of pupils.
    12	Results. Motor traffic on the closed streets fell by 76% during the restriction hours. Mean
    13	NO2 at the school gates fell by 14.3%, and the share of pupils walking, cycling or scooting
    14	to school rose by nine percentage points. Traffic on the boundary roads rose slightly.
    15	Conclusions. The pilot reduced traffic and air pollution outside the schools with little
    16	evidence of displacement onto other roads. We recommend that the scheme be made permanent at
    17	all 12 sites.
    18	Keywords: school streets; timed road closure; nitrogen dioxide; active travel; traffic
    19	displacement.
    20	
    21	1 Introduction
    22	Traffic outside schools at drop-off and pick-up times raises concerns about road danger,
    23	congestion and children's exposure to air pollution. Children may be particularly vulnerable
    24	to traffic-related pollution because they breathe faster than adults and spend time close to
    25	the height of vehicle exhausts. Brackenford's 2023 Transport Strategy committed the council
    26	to test measures that make the journey to school safer and healthier.
    27	This report evaluates the School Streets pilot, which began in September 2024. It sets out
    28	the effects of the pilot on motor traffic in the closed streets, on NO2 concentrations, on
    29	how pupils travel to school and on traffic in the wider road network, and it reports the
    30	views of parents and residents. The report is intended to inform the council's decision on
    31	whether to make the scheme permanent.
    32	The pilot forms part of a wider programme to reduce car use for short journeys in the
    33	borough. Most primary pupils in Brackenford live within walking distance of their school,
    34	yet many are driven, and head teachers have reported repeated complaints about parking on
    35	pavements and across driveways at the start and end of the school day.
    36	2 Background and previous studies
    37	School Streets have spread rapidly since 2017, and a growing number of evaluations have been
    38	published. In a study of 37 schemes in a large capital city, Rowland and Tait (2021)
    39	reported that NO2 at the school gate fell by up to 23% during the morning drop-off period.
    40	Kerrigan and colleagues (2022) studied 18 sites in northern England and found that traffic
    41	on boundary roads rose by 4% on average, with no measurable change in NO2 on those roads.
    42	Effects on travel behaviour have also varied. Abbott (2020) reported that the share of
    43	pupils driven to school fell from 31% to 24% across a programme of 22 schools, while Pereira
    44	and Lund (2022) found no change in car use at schools where the closures were staffed by
    45	volunteers rather than enforced by cameras. Daley and Moss (2023) reviewed 14 evaluations
    46	and found that parental support for making schemes permanent ranged from 63% to 81%.
    47	Most published studies have been short, have lacked a comparison period in the same months
    48	of the year, or have measured air quality at only one or two sites. The present evaluation
    49	was designed to address these gaps by using a full baseline period and by monitoring at
    50	every pilot school.
    51	
    52	3 Methods
    53	3.1 Design and sites
    54	The evaluation used a before-and-after design with matched calendar months. The baseline
    55	period ran from January to June 2024 and the pilot period from January to June 2025, so that
    56	seasonal differences in weather and traffic were balanced. The 12 participating primary
    57	schools were selected from 31 schools that applied, on the basis of traffic volume, road
    58	layout and the agreement of the head teacher.
    59	3.2 The intervention
    60	At each school, the street outside the main entrance was closed to motor traffic from 08:15
    61	to 09:15 and from 14:45 to 15:45 on school days. Residents, blue badge holders and essential
    62	services could apply for an exemption. The closures were enforced by automatic number plate
    63	recognition cameras, and drivers without an exemption received a warning letter during the
    64	first four weeks and a penalty charge notice after that. Signs and planters marked the
    65	closure points, and school staff were asked not to act as marshals.
    66	3.3 Measurements
    67	Motor vehicles entering each closed street during the restriction hours were counted by the
    68	enforcement cameras on every school day. Traffic on eight boundary roads, the main roads to
    69	which diverted vehicles were expected to move, was counted with pneumatic tube counters for
    70	two weeks in each month. The tube counters were checked against manual counts on one morning
    71	in each month.
    72	NO2 was measured with passive diffusion tubes exposed for one month at a time at the gate of
    73	each school, at the eight boundary road sites and at three urban background sites away from
    74	main roads. Results were bias-adjusted using a co-location study at the council's reference
    75	monitoring station. Continuous monitors that record hourly NO2 values were also installed at
    76	four schools.
    77	Pupils' usual mode of travel to school was recorded with a hands-up survey in each class in
    78	March 2024 and March 2025. Parents, and residents living within 200 metres of a pilot
    79	school, were invited to complete an online survey in May 2025.
    80	3.4 Analysis
    81	Changes are reported as differences between the pilot and baseline period means. To separate
    82	the effect of the pilot from borough-wide trends, the change at the school gates was
    83	adjusted for the change at the urban background sites using a ratio method. Confidence
    84	intervals were obtained by bootstrapping over sites. Survey results are reported as
    85	percentages of the pupils present on the survey day, and no weighting was applied.
    86	
    87	3.5 Ethics and data protection
    88	The council's research governance group approved the evaluation. Camera data were used only
    89	as anonymous counts, and the surveys did not collect names or addresses.
    90	4 Results
    91	4.1 Traffic on the closed streets
    92	Compliance with the closures improved steadily once penalty charge notices were introduced.
    93	Across the 12 sites, the mean number of motor vehicles entering the closed streets during
    94	the restriction hours fell from 214 to 62 per school day, a reduction of 71%. This reduction
    95	was achieved at every site, although the vehicles that remained were mostly exempt at some
    96	schools and mostly non-exempt at others.
    97	Table 1 shows that the morning and afternoon restriction hours saw similar reductions.
    98	Exempt vehicles made up 38% of the traffic that remained during the pilot.
    99	Table 1. Mean motor vehicles entering the closed streets per school day, all 12 sites
   100	Restriction period Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   101	Morning, 08:15 to 09:15 118 33 -72
   102	Afternoon, 14:45 to 15:45 96 29 -70
   103	Both periods 214 62 -71
   104	4.2 Nitrogen dioxide at the school gates
   105	NO2 fell at all 12 school gates. Mean NO2 at the school gates fell from 31.4 micrograms per
   106	cubic metre (ug/m3) in the baseline period to 26.9 ug/m3 in the pilot period, a reduction of
   107	14.3%. Concentrations also fell at the urban background sites, reflecting changes in the
   108	vehicle fleet and other borough-wide trends.
   109	After adjustment for the change at the urban background sites, the reduction in NO2 at the
   110	school gates attributable to the pilot was estimated at 10.6% (95% CI 5.2 to 15.7).
   111	
   112	Table 2 compares the school gates with the boundary road and urban background monitoring
   113	sites.
   114	Table 2. Mean NO2 concentration by monitoring location, January to June, ug/m3
   115	Location type Sites Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   116	School gate 12 31.4 26.9 -14.3
   117	Boundary road 8 35.2 35.8 +1.7
   118	Urban background 3 21.6 20.7 -4.2
   119	No school gate site exceeded the annual mean objective of 40 ug/m3 in either period,
   120	although two were within 5 ug/m3 of it at baseline.
   121	The fall at the school gates was seen in every month of the pilot period. It was largest in
   122	February and smallest in June, when concentrations are lowest at all types of site.
   123	4.3 Hourly patterns
   124	Continuous monitors at four schools recorded hourly NO2 concentrations. During the morning
   125	restriction hour, mean NO2 at these four schools was 21% lower than in the baseline period.
   126	The afternoon restriction hour showed a smaller fall of 12%, and outside the restriction
   127	hours the fall was 6%. Because continuous monitors were installed at only four of the twelve
   128	schools, these hourly results may not be representative of all pilot sites.
   129	The concentration of the fall in the restriction hours is consistent with the pilot being
   130	its cause, rather than a general improvement in air quality across the borough.
   131	
   132	4.4 Travel to school
   133	The share of pupils who usually walked, cycled or scooted to school rose from 58% in the
   134	baseline survey to 67% in the pilot survey. These gains were concentrated among pupils
   135	living within one kilometre of the school, while travel by pupils living further away
   136	changed little.
   137	The follow-up survey was completed at only 10 of the 12 schools, because two schools were
   138	unable to run it before the end of term. Baseline results are therefore shown for the same
   139	10 schools.
   140	Table 3. Usual mode of travel to school, percentage of pupils, 10 schools
   141	Mode Baseline March 2024 Pilot March 2025
   142	Walk 49 55
   143	Cycle 3 5
   144	Scooter 6 7
   145	Car 34 25
   146	Bus 6 6
   147	Other 2 2
   148	Parents who had stopped driving most often said that the closure made walking feel safer or
   149	that parking near the school had become more difficult. Some parents reported parking
   150	further away and walking the last part of the journey, which the survey recorded as walking.
   151	
   152	4.5 Traffic on boundary roads
   153	Some drivers who previously used the closed streets diverted to the surrounding main roads.
   154	Across the eight boundary roads, traffic during the restriction hours increased by 6.2%
   155	compared with the baseline period. However, this increase was within the range of normal
   156	year-to-year variation recorded at the borough's permanent traffic counters, which is plus
   157	or minus 8%.
   158	The largest increase, 11%, was on Mill Road next to Crossley Road Primary, where the closed
   159	street had previously carried the most traffic. Outside the restriction hours, traffic on
   160	the boundary roads was unchanged.
   161	4.6 Views of parents and residents
   162	The online survey received 1,206 responses from parents and 388 from residents. Among
   163	parents, 73% supported making the School Street at their child's school permanent, and 18%
   164	were opposed. Among residents, 54% supported a permanent scheme and 37% were opposed.
   165	The resident survey had a response rate of 23%, so these results may not reflect the views
   166	of all residents. Residents who opposed the scheme most often mentioned difficulty with
   167	deliveries and visitors, while supporters most often mentioned quieter streets.
   168	4.7 Enforcement
   169	Penalty charge notices were issued throughout the pilot, but most were issued in the first
   170	half term, and the number fell steadily as drivers became familiar with the closures.
   171	Exemption permits were most often held by residents of the closed streets.
   172	
   173	5 Discussion
   174	The pilot achieved large reductions in motor traffic on the closed streets and a measurable
   175	improvement in air quality at the school gates. The adjusted reduction in NO2 of 10.6% is
   176	smaller than the 23% reported by Rowland and Tait (2021), but their figure referred to the
   177	morning peak only, and our hourly data for the morning restriction hour show a comparable
   178	fall.
   179	The rise in active travel was smaller than in some earlier programmes but was achieved
   180	without volunteer marshals. The evidence of traffic displacement was weak: traffic on
   181	boundary roads rose by a modest amount, and NO2 on those roads was essentially unchanged.
   182	Parental support of 73% is within the range reported by Daley and Moss (2023).
   183	For the council, the main practical lessons concern enforcement and exemptions. Camera
   184	enforcement allowed the closures to operate without staff at the barriers, and a simple
   185	online exemption process kept complaints from residents to a manageable level. Schools on
   186	busier roads, where a closure would divert large volumes of traffic, may need a different
   187	approach.
   188	6 Limitations
   189	The evaluation has several limitations. It used a before-and-after design without control
   190	schools, so other changes between 2024 and 2025 may have contributed to the results,
   191	although the adjustment for background NO2 addresses part of this. Diffusion tubes give
   192	monthly averages and cannot show exposure during the restriction hours at most sites.
   193	The study did not measure health outcomes, such as asthma symptoms or hospital admissions
   194	among pupils, and the pilot period was too short to assess changes in road traffic
   195	collisions. The travel survey relied on pupils' reports of their usual mode of travel and
   196	was not completed at all schools.
   197	
   198	7 Conclusions and recommendations
   199	School Streets reduced motor traffic and NO2 outside the 12 pilot schools and were
   200	associated with more pupils walking, cycling or scooting to school. We recommend that the
   201	council makes the scheme permanent at all 12 schools, continues monitoring on the boundary
   202	roads for a further year, and extends School Streets to suitable schools on the waiting
   203	list.
   204	Acknowledgements
   205	We thank the head teachers, staff, pupils and parents of the 12 pilot schools, the council's
   206	parking enforcement team, and the volunteers who helped to change the diffusion tubes each
   207	month.
   208	Funding
   209	The evaluation was funded by a grant from the Regional Active Travel Fund. The funder had no
   210	role in the design of the evaluation, the analysis or the decision to publish.
   211	References
   212	Abbott J (2020). Changing the school run: results from a 22-school programme. Urban Mobility
   213	Review 6: 100-112.
   214	Daley R, Moss K (2023). Public support for School Streets: a review of 14 evaluations. Urban
   215	Mobility Review 9: 44-58.
   216	Kerrigan P, Shaw L, Udeh C (2022). Traffic displacement near School Streets in northern
   217	England. Transport Policy Studies 31: 210-224.
   218	Pereira A, Lund M (2022). Volunteer-staffed and camera-enforced school streets compared.
   219	Local Transport Research 7: 15-29.
   220	Rowland S, Tait H (2021). Air quality at the school gate: evidence from 37 School Streets.
   221	City Air Quality Journal 4: 77-90.
   222	Data availability
   223	Anonymised traffic counts and diffusion tube results are available from the Transport Policy
   224	and Research Team on request.
   225	Appendix A. Pilot schools
   226	
   227	The 12 pilot schools were Ashgrove Primary, Beckside Primary, Crossley Road Primary, Dunmore
   228	Infant School, Elmfield Primary, Fairholme Junior School, Greystone Primary, Hollins Lane
   229	Primary, Ivydale Primary, Juniper Hill Primary, Kingsmead Primary and Larkrise Primary.
   230	Site-level traffic and NO2 results are held in the accompanying site data workbook.

    60	At each school, the street outside the main entrance was closed to motor traffic from 08:15
    61	to 09:15 and from 14:45 to 15:45 on school days. Residents, blue badge holders and essential
    62	services could apply for an exemption. The closures were enforced by automatic number plate
    63	recognition cameras, and drivers without an exemption received a warning letter during the
    64	first four weeks and a penalty charge notice after that. Signs and planters marked the
    65	closure points, and school staff were asked not to act as marshals.
    66	3.3 Measurements
    67	Motor vehicles entering each closed street during the restriction hours were counted by the
    68	enforcement cameras on every school day. Traffic on eight boundary roads, the main roads to
    69	which diverted vehicles were expected to move, was counted with pneumatic tube counters for
    70	two weeks in each month. The tube counters were checked against manual counts on one morning
    71	in each month.
    72	NO2 was measured with passive diffusion tubes exposed for one month at a time at the gate of
    73	each school, at the eight boundary road sites and at three urban background sites away from
    74	main roads. Results were bias-adjusted using a co-location study at the council's reference
    75	monitoring station. Continuous monitors that record hourly NO2 values were also installed at
    76	four schools.
    77	Pupils' usual mode of travel to school was recorded with a hands-up survey in each class in
    78	March 2024 and March 2025. Parents, and residents living within 200 metres of a pilot
    79	school, were invited to complete an online survey in May 2025.
    80	3.4 Analysis
    81	Changes are reported as differences between the pilot and baseline period means. To separate
    82	the effect of the pilot from borough-wide trends, the change at the school gates was
    83	adjusted for the change at the urban background sites using a ratio method. Confidence
    84	intervals were obtained by bootstrapping over sites. Survey results are reported as
    85	percentages of the pupils present on the survey day, and no weighting was applied.
    86	
    87	3.5 Ethics and data protection
    88	The council's research governance group approved the evaluation. Camera data were used only
    89	as anonymous counts, and the surveys did not collect names or addresses.
    90	4 Results
    91	4.1 Traffic on the closed streets
    92	Compliance with the closures improved steadily once penalty charge notices were introduced.
    93	Across the 12 sites, the mean number of motor vehicles entering the closed streets during
    94	the restriction hours fell from 214 to 62 per school day, a reduction of 71%. This reduction
    95	was achieved at every site, although the vehicles that remained were mostly exempt at some
    96	schools and mostly non-exempt at others.
    97	Table 1 shows that the morning and afternoon restriction hours saw similar reductions.
    98	Exempt vehicles made up 38% of the traffic that remained during the pilot.
    99	Table 1. Mean motor vehicles entering the closed streets per school day, all 12 sites
   100	Restriction period Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   101	Morning, 08:15 to 09:15 118 33 -72
   102	Afternoon, 14:45 to 15:45 96 29 -70
   103	Both periods 214 62 -71
   104	4.2 Nitrogen dioxide at the school gates
   105	NO2 fell at all 12 school gates. Mean NO2 at the school gates fell from 31.4 micrograms per
   106	cubic metre (ug/m3) in the baseline period to 26.9 ug/m3 in the pilot period, a reduction of
   107	14.3%. Concentrations also fell at the urban background sites, reflecting changes in the
   108	vehicle fleet and other borough-wide trends.
   109	After adjustment for the change at the urban background sites, the reduction in NO2 at the
   110	school gates attributable to the pilot was estimated at 10.6% (95% CI 5.2 to 15.7).
   111	
   112	Table 2 compares the school gates with the boundary road and urban background monitoring
   113	sites.
   114	Table 2. Mean NO2 concentration by monitoring location, January to June, ug/m3
   115	Location type Sites Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   116	School gate 12 31.4 26.9 -14.3
   117	Boundary road 8 35.2 35.8 +1.7
   118	Urban background 3 21.6 20.7 -4.2
   119	No school gate site exceeded the annual mean objective of 40 ug/m3 in either period,
   120	although two were within 5 ug/m3 of it at baseline.
   121	The fall at the school gates was seen in every month of the pilot period. It was largest in
   122	February and smallest in June, when concentrations are lowest at all types of site.
   123	4.3 Hourly patterns
   124	Continuous monitors at four schools recorded hourly NO2 concentrations. During the morning
   125	restriction hour, mean NO2 at these four schools was 21% lower than in the baseline period.
   126	The afternoon restriction hour showed a smaller fall of 12%, and outside the restriction
   127	hours the fall was 6%. Because continuous monitors were installed at only four of the twelve
   128	schools, these hourly results may not be representative of all pilot sites.
   129	The concentration of the fall in the restriction hours is consistent with the pilot being
   130	its cause, rather than a general improvement in air quality across the borough.
   131	
   132	4.4 Travel to school
   133	The share of pupils who usually walked, cycled or scooted to school rose from 58% in the
   134	baseline survey to 67% in the pilot survey. These gains were concentrated among pupils
   135	living within one kilometre of the school, while travel by pupils living further away
   136	changed little.
   137	The follow-up survey was completed at only 10 of the 12 schools, because two schools were
   138	unable to run it before the end of term. Baseline results are therefore shown for the same
   139	10 schools.

     1	School Streets Pilot Evaluation: Traffic, Air Quality and Travel to School
     2	Final report, October 2025. Prepared by the Transport Policy and Research Team, Brackenford
     3	Borough Council, with the Centre for Urban Air Research, University of Westmoor.
     4	Abstract
     5	Background. School Streets are timed road closures that restrict motor traffic on the street
     6	outside a school at the start and end of the school day. Brackenford Borough Council piloted
     7	School Streets at 12 primary schools during the 2024 to 2025 school year.
     8	Methods. We compared the pilot period, January to June 2025, with a baseline period covering
     9	the same months of 2024. Motor traffic was counted by automatic number plate recognition
    10	cameras, nitrogen dioxide (NO2) was measured with diffusion tubes at each school gate and on
    11	nearby boundary roads, and travel to school was recorded in hands-up surveys of pupils.
    12	Results. Motor traffic on the closed streets fell by 76% during the restriction hours. Mean
    13	NO2 at the school gates fell by 14.3%, and the share of pupils walking, cycling or scooting
    14	to school rose by nine percentage points. Traffic on the boundary roads rose slightly.
    15	Conclusions. The pilot reduced traffic and air pollution outside the schools with little
    16	evidence of displacement onto other roads. We recommend that the scheme be made permanent at
    17	all 12 sites.
    18	Keywords: school streets; timed road closure; nitrogen dioxide; active travel; traffic
    19	displacement.
    20	
    21	1 Introduction
    22	Traffic outside schools at drop-off and pick-up times raises concerns about road danger,
    23	congestion and children's exposure to air pollution. Children may be particularly vulnerable
    24	to traffic-related pollution because they breathe faster than adults and spend time close to
    25	the height of vehicle exhausts. Brackenford's 2023 Transport Strategy committed the council
    26	to test measures that make the journey to school safer and healthier.
    27	This report evaluates the School Streets pilot, which began in September 2024. It sets out
    28	the effects of the pilot on motor traffic in the closed streets, on NO2 concentrations, on
    29	how pupils travel to school and on traffic in the wider road network, and it reports the
    30	views of parents and residents. The report is intended to inform the council's decision on
    31	whether to make the scheme permanent.
    32	The pilot forms part of a wider programme to reduce car use for short journeys in the
    33	borough. Most primary pupils in Brackenford live within walking distance of their school,
    34	yet many are driven, and head teachers have reported repeated complaints about parking on
    35	pavements and across driveways at the start and end of the school day.
    36	2 Background and previous studies
    37	School Streets have spread rapidly since 2017, and a growing number of evaluations have been
    38	published. In a study of 37 schemes in a large capital city, Rowland and Tait (2021)
    39	reported that NO2 at the school gate fell by up to 23% during the morning drop-off period.
    40	Kerrigan and colleagues (2022) studied 18 sites in northern England and found that traffic
    41	on boundary roads rose by 4% on average, with no measurable change in NO2 on those roads.
    42	Effects on travel behaviour have also varied. Abbott (2020) reported that the share of
    43	pupils driven to school fell from 31% to 24% across a programme of 22 schools, while Pereira
    44	and Lund (2022) found no change in car use at schools where the closures were staffed by
    45	volunteers rather than enforced by cameras. Daley and Moss (2023) reviewed 14 evaluations
    46	and found that parental support for making schemes permanent ranged from 63% to 81%.
    47	Most published studies have been short, have lacked a comparison period in the same months
    48	of the year, or have measured air quality at only one or two sites. The present evaluation
    49	was designed to address these gaps by using a full baseline period and by monitoring at
    50	every pilot school.
    51	
    52	3 Methods
    53	3.1 Design and sites
    54	The evaluation used a before-and-after design with matched calendar months. The baseline
    55	period ran from January to June 2024 and the pilot period from January to June 2025, so that
    56	seasonal differences in weather and traffic were balanced. The 12 participating primary
    57	schools were selected from 31 schools that applied, on the basis of traffic volume, road
    58	layout and the agreement of the head teacher.
    59	3.2 The intervention
    60	At each school, the street outside the main entrance was closed to motor traffic from 08:15
    61	to 09:15 and from 14:45 to 15:45 on school days. Residents, blue badge holders and essential
    62	services could apply for an exemption. The closures were enforced by automatic number plate
    63	recognition cameras, and drivers without an exemption received a warning letter during the
    64	first four weeks and a penalty charge notice after that. Signs and planters marked the
    65	closure points, and school staff were asked not to act as marshals.
    66	3.3 Measurements
    67	Motor vehicles entering each closed street during the restriction hours were counted by the
    68	enforcement cameras on every school day. Traffic on eight boundary roads, the main roads to
    69	which diverted vehicles were expected to move, was counted with pneumatic tube counters for
    70	two weeks in each month. The tube counters were checked against manual counts on one morning
    71	in each month.
    72	NO2 was measured with passive diffusion tubes exposed for one month at a time at the gate of
    73	each school, at the eight boundary road sites and at three urban background sites away from
    74	main roads. Results were bias-adjusted using a co-location study at the council's reference
    75	monitoring station. Continuous monitors that record hourly NO2 values were also installed at
    76	four schools.
    77	Pupils' usual mode of travel to school was recorded with a hands-up survey in each class in
    78	March 2024 and March 2025. Parents, and residents living within 200 metres of a pilot
    79	school, were invited to complete an online survey in May 2025.
    80	3.4 Analysis
    81	Changes are reported as differences between the pilot and baseline period means. To separate
    82	the effect of the pilot from borough-wide trends, the change at the school gates was
    83	adjusted for the change at the urban background sites using a ratio method. Confidence
    84	intervals were obtained by bootstrapping over sites. Survey results are reported as
    85	percentages of the pupils present on the survey day, and no weighting was applied.
    86	
    87	3.5 Ethics and data protection
    88	The council's research governance group approved the evaluation. Camera data were used only
    89	as anonymous counts, and the surveys did not collect names or addresses.
    90	4 Results
    91	4.1 Traffic on the closed streets
    92	Compliance with the closures improved steadily once penalty charge notices were introduced.
    93	Across the 12 sites, the mean number of motor vehicles entering the closed streets during
    94	the restriction hours fell from 214 to 62 per school day, a reduction of 71%. This reduction
    95	was achieved at every site, although the vehicles that remained were mostly exempt at some
    96	schools and mostly non-exempt at others.
    97	Table 1 shows that the morning and afternoon restriction hours saw similar reductions.
    98	Exempt vehicles made up 38% of the traffic that remained during the pilot.
    99	Table 1. Mean motor vehicles entering the closed streets per school day, all 12 sites
   100	Restriction period Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   101	Morning, 08:15 to 09:15 118 33 -72
   102	Afternoon, 14:45 to 15:45 96 29 -70
   103	Both periods 214 62 -71
   104	4.2 Nitrogen dioxide at the school gates
   105	NO2 fell at all 12 school gates. Mean NO2 at the school gates fell from 31.4 micrograms per
   106	cubic metre (ug/m3) in the baseline period to 26.9 ug/m3 in the pilot period, a reduction of
   107	14.3%. Concentrations also fell at the urban background sites, reflecting changes in the
   108	vehicle fleet and other borough-wide trends.
   109	After adjustment for the change at the urban background sites, the reduction in NO2 at the
   110	school gates attributable to the pilot was estimated at 10.6% (95% CI 5.2 to 15.7).
   111	
   112	Table 2 compares the school gates with the boundary road and urban background monitoring
   113	sites.
   114	Table 2. Mean NO2 concentration by monitoring location, January to June, ug/m3
   115	Location type Sites Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   116	School gate 12 31.4 26.9 -14.3
   117	Boundary road 8 35.2 35.8 +1.7
   118	Urban background 3 21.6 20.7 -4.2
   119	No school gate site exceeded the annual mean objective of 40 ug/m3 in either period,
   120	although two were within 5 ug/m3 of it at baseline.
   121	The fall at the school gates was seen in every month of the pilot period. It was largest in
   122	February and smallest in June, when concentrations are lowest at all types of site.
   123	4.3 Hourly patterns
   124	Continuous monitors at four schools recorded hourly NO2 concentrations. During the morning
   125	restriction hour, mean NO2 at these four schools was 21% lower than in the baseline period.
   126	The afternoon restriction hour showed a smaller fall of 12%, and outside the restriction
   127	hours the fall was 6%. Because continuous monitors were installed at only four of the twelve
   128	schools, these hourly results may not be representative of all pilot sites.
   129	The concentration of the fall in the restriction hours is consistent with the pilot being
   130	its cause, rather than a general improvement in air quality across the borough.
   131	
   132	4.4 Travel to school
   133	The share of pupils who usually walked, cycled or scooted to school rose from 58% in the
   134	baseline survey to 67% in the pilot survey. These gains were concentrated among pupils
   135	living within one kilometre of the school, while travel by pupils living further away
   136	changed little.
   137	The follow-up survey was completed at only 10 of the 12 schools, because two schools were
   138	unable to run it before the end of term. Baseline results are therefore shown for the same
   139	10 schools.
   140	Table 3. Usual mode of travel to school, percentage of pupils, 10 schools
   141	Mode Baseline March 2024 Pilot March 2025
   142	Walk 49 55
   143	Cycle 3 5
   144	Scooter 6 7
   145	Car 34 25
   146	Bus 6 6
   147	Other 2 2
   148	Parents who had stopped driving most often said that the closure made walking feel safer or
   149	that parking near the school had become more difficult. Some parents reported parking
   150	further away and walking the last part of the journey, which the survey recorded as walking.
   151	
   152	4.5 Traffic on boundary roads
   153	Some drivers who previously used the closed streets diverted to the surrounding main roads.
   154	Across the eight boundary roads, traffic during the restriction hours increased by 6.2%
   155	compared with the baseline period. However, this increase was within the range of normal
   156	year-to-year variation recorded at the borough's permanent traffic counters, which is plus
   157	or minus 8%.
   158	The largest increase, 11%, was on Mill Road next to Crossley Road Primary, where the closed
   159	street had previously carried the most traffic. Outside the restriction hours, traffic on
   160	the boundary roads was unchanged.
   161	4.6 Views of parents and residents
   162	The online survey received 1,206 responses from parents and 388 from residents. Among
   163	parents, 73% supported making the School Street at their child's school permanent, and 18%
   164	were opposed. Among residents, 54% supported a permanent scheme and 37% were opposed.
   165	The resident survey had a response rate of 23%, so these results may not reflect the views
   166	of all residents. Residents who opposed the scheme most often mentioned difficulty with
   167	deliveries and visitors, while supporters most often mentioned quieter streets.
   168	4.7 Enforcement
   169	Penalty charge notices were issued throughout the pilot, but most were issued in the first
   170	half term, and the number fell steadily as drivers became familiar with the closures.
   171	Exemption permits were most often held by residents of the closed streets.
   172	
   173	5 Discussion
   174	The pilot achieved large reductions in motor traffic on the closed streets and a measurable
   175	improvement in air quality at the school gates. The adjusted reduction in NO2 of 10.6% is
   176	smaller than the 23% reported by Rowland and Tait (2021), but their figure referred to the
   177	morning peak only, and our hourly data for the morning restriction hour show a comparable
   178	fall.
   179	The rise in active travel was smaller than in some earlier programmes but was achieved
   180	without volunteer marshals. The evidence of traffic displacement was weak: traffic on
   181	boundary roads rose by a modest amount, and NO2 on those roads was essentially unchanged.
   182	Parental support of 73% is within the range reported by Daley and Moss (2023).
   183	For the council, the main practical lessons concern enforcement and exemptions. Camera
   184	enforcement allowed the closures to operate without staff at the barriers, and a simple
   185	online exemption process kept complaints from residents to a manageable level. Schools on
   186	busier roads, where a closure would divert large volumes of traffic, may need a different
   187	approach.
   188	6 Limitations
   189	The evaluation has several limitations. It used a before-and-after design without control
   190	schools, so other changes between 2024 and 2025 may have contributed to the results,
   191	although the adjustment for background NO2 addresses part of this. Diffusion tubes give
   192	monthly averages and cannot show exposure during the restriction hours at most sites.
   193	The study did not measure health outcomes, such as asthma symptoms or hospital admissions
   194	among pupils, and the pilot period was too short to assess changes in road traffic
   195	collisions. The travel survey relied on pupils' reports of their usual mode of travel and
   196	was not completed at all schools.
   197	
   198	7 Conclusions and recommendations
   199	School Streets reduced motor traffic and NO2 outside the 12 pilot schools and were
   200	associated with more pupils walking, cycling or scooting to school. We recommend that the
   201	council makes the scheme permanent at all 12 schools, continues monitoring on the boundary
   202	roads for a further year, and extends School Streets to suitable schools on the waiting
   203	list.
   204	Acknowledgements
   205	We thank the head teachers, staff, pupils and parents of the 12 pilot schools, the council's
   206	parking enforcement team, and the volunteers who helped to change the diffusion tubes each
   207	month.
   208	Funding
   209	The evaluation was funded by a grant from the Regional Active Travel Fund. The funder had no
   210	role in the design of the evaluation, the analysis or the decision to publish.
   211	References
   212	Abbott J (2020). Changing the school run: results from a 22-school programme. Urban Mobility
   213	Review 6: 100-112.
   214	Daley R, Moss K (2023). Public support for School Streets: a review of 14 evaluations. Urban
   215	Mobility Review 9: 44-58.
   216	Kerrigan P, Shaw L, Udeh C (2022). Traffic displacement near School Streets in northern
   217	England. Transport Policy Studies 31: 210-224.
   218	Pereira A, Lund M (2022). Volunteer-staffed and camera-enforced school streets compared.
   219	Local Transport Research 7: 15-29.
   220	Rowland S, Tait H (2021). Air quality at the school gate: evidence from 37 School Streets.
   221	City Air Quality Journal 4: 77-90.
   222	Data availability
   223	Anonymised traffic counts and diffusion tube results are available from the Transport Policy
   224	and Research Team on request.

   226	
   227	The 12 pilot schools were Ashgrove Primary, Beckside Primary, Crossley Road Primary, Dunmore
   228	Infant School, Elmfield Primary, Fairholme Junior School, Greystone Primary, Hollins Lane
   229	Primary, Ivydale Primary, Juniper Hill Primary, Kingsmead Primary and Larkrise Primary.

Evaluations/School Streets pilot evaluation report.pdf
     1	School Streets Pilot Evaluation: Traffic, Air Quality and Travel to School
     2	Final report, October 2025. Prepared by the Transport Policy and Research Team, Brackenford
     3	Borough Council, with the Centre for Urban Air Research, University of Westmoor.
     4	Abstract
     5	Background. School Streets are timed road closures that restrict motor traffic on the street
     6	outside a school at the start and end of the school day. Brackenford Borough Council piloted
     7	School Streets at 12 primary schools during the 2024 to 2025 school year.
     8	Methods. We compared the pilot period, January to June 2025, with a baseline period covering
     9	the same months of 2024. Motor traffic was counted by automatic number plate recognition
    10	cameras, nitrogen dioxide (NO2) was measured with diffusion tubes at each school gate and on
    11	nearby boundary roads, and travel to school was recorded in hands-up surveys of pupils.
    12	Results. Motor traffic on the closed streets fell by 76% during the restriction hours. Mean
    13	NO2 at the school gates fell by 14.3%, and the share of pupils walking, cycling or scooting
    14	to school rose by nine percentage points. Traffic on the boundary roads rose slightly.
    15	Conclusions. The pilot reduced traffic and air pollution outside the schools with little
    16	evidence of displacement onto other roads. We recommend that the scheme be made permanent at
    17	all 12 sites.
    18	Keywords: school streets; timed road closure; nitrogen dioxide; active travel; traffic
    19	displacement.
    20	
    21	1 Introduction
    22	Traffic outside schools at drop-off and pick-up times raises concerns about road danger,
    23	congestion and children's exposure to air pollution. Children may be particularly vulnerable
    24	to traffic-related pollution because they breathe faster than adults and spend time close to
    25	the height of vehicle exhausts. Brackenford's 2023 Transport Strategy committed the council
    26	to test measures that make the journey to school safer and healthier.
    27	This report evaluates the School Streets pilot, which began in September 2024. It sets out
    28	the effects of the pilot on motor traffic in the closed streets, on NO2 concentrations, on
    29	how pupils travel to school and on traffic in the wider road network, and it reports the
    30	views of parents and residents. The report is intended to inform the council's decision on
    31	whether to make the scheme permanent.
    32	The pilot forms part of a wider programme to reduce car use for short journeys in the
    33	borough. Most primary pupils in Brackenford live within walking distance of their school,
    34	yet many are driven, and head teachers have reported repeated complaints about parking on
    35	pavements and across driveways at the start and end of the school day.
    36	2 Background and previous studies
    37	School Streets have spread rapidly since 2017, and a growing number of evaluations have been
    38	published. In a study of 37 schemes in a large capital city, Rowland and Tait (2021)
    39	reported that NO2 at the school gate fell by up to 23% during the morning drop-off period.
    40	Kerrigan and colleagues (2022) studied 18 sites in northern England and found that traffic
    41	on boundary roads rose by 4% on average, with no measurable change in NO2 on those roads.
    42	Effects on travel behaviour have also varied. Abbott (2020) reported that the share of
    43	pupils driven to school fell from 31% to 24% across a programme of 22 schools, while Pereira
    44	and Lund (2022) found no change in car use at schools where the closures were staffed by
    45	volunteers rather than enforced by cameras. Daley and Moss (2023) reviewed 14 evaluations
    46	and found that parental support for making schemes permanent ranged from 63% to 81%.
    47	Most published studies have been short, have lacked a comparison period in the same months
    48	of the year, or have measured air quality at only one or two sites. The present evaluation
    49	was designed to address these gaps by using a full baseline period and by monitoring at
    50	every pilot school.
    51	
    52	3 Methods
    53	3.1 Design and sites
    54	The evaluation used a before-and-after design with matched calendar months. The baseline
    55	period ran from January to June 2024 and the pilot period from January to June 2025, so that
    56	seasonal differences in weather and traffic were balanced. The 12 participating primary
    57	schools were selected from 31 schools that applied, on the basis of traffic volume, road
    58	layout and the agreement of the head teacher.
    59	3.2 The intervention
    60	At each school, the street outside the main entrance was closed to motor traffic from 08:15
    61	to 09:15 and from 14:45 to 15:45 on school days. Residents, blue badge holders and essential
    62	services could apply for an exemption. The closures were enforced by automatic number plate
    63	recognition cameras, and drivers without an exemption received a warning letter during the
    64	first four weeks and a penalty charge notice after that. Signs and planters marked the
    65	closure points, and school staff were asked not to act as marshals.
    66	3.3 Measurements
    67	Motor vehicles entering each closed street during the restriction hours were counted by the
    68	enforcement cameras on every school day. Traffic on eight boundary roads, the main roads to
    69	which diverted vehicles were expected to move, was counted with pneumatic tube counters for
    70	two weeks in each month. The tube counters were checked against manual counts on one morning
    71	in each month.
    72	NO2 was measured with passive diffusion tubes exposed for one month at a time at the gate of
    73	each school, at the eight boundary road sites and at three urban background sites away from
    74	main roads. Results were bias-adjusted using a co-location study at the council's reference
    75	monitoring station. Continuous monitors that record hourly NO2 values were also installed at
    76	four schools.
    77	Pupils' usual mode of travel to school was recorded with a hands-up survey in each class in
    78	March 2024 and March 2025. Parents, and residents living within 200 metres of a pilot
    79	school, were invited to complete an online survey in May 2025.
    80	3.4 Analysis
    81	Changes are reported as differences between the pilot and baseline period means. To separate
    82	the effect of the pilot from borough-wide trends, the change at the school gates was
    83	adjusted for the change at the urban background sites using a ratio method. Confidence
    84	intervals were obtained by bootstrapping over sites. Survey results are reported as
    85	percentages of the pupils present on the survey day, and no weighting was applied.
    86	
    87	3.5 Ethics and data protection
    88	The council's research governance group approved the evaluation. Camera data were used only
    89	as anonymous counts, and the surveys did not collect names or addresses.
    90	4 Results
    91	4.1 Traffic on the closed streets
    92	Compliance with the closures improved steadily once penalty charge notices were introduced.
    93	Across the 12 sites, the mean number of motor vehicles entering the closed streets during
    94	the restriction hours fell from 214 to 62 per school day, a reduction of 71%. This reduction
    95	was achieved at every site, although the vehicles that remained were mostly exempt at some
    96	schools and mostly non-exempt at others.
    97	Table 1 shows that the morning and afternoon restriction hours saw similar reductions.
    98	Exempt vehicles made up 38% of the traffic that remained during the pilot.
    99	Table 1. Mean motor vehicles entering the closed streets per school day, all 12 sites
   100	Restriction period Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   101	Morning, 08:15 to 09:15 118 33 -72
   102	Afternoon, 14:45 to 15:45 96 29 -70
   103	Both periods 214 62 -71
   104	4.2 Nitrogen dioxide at the school gates
   105	NO2 fell at all 12 school gates. Mean NO2 at the school gates fell from 31.4 micrograms per
   106	cubic metre (ug/m3) in the baseline period to 26.9 ug/m3 in the pilot period, a reduction of
   107	14.3%. Concentrations also fell at the urban background sites, reflecting changes in the
   108	vehicle fleet and other borough-wide trends.
   109	After adjustment for the change at the urban background sites, the reduction in NO2 at the
   110	school gates attributable to the pilot was estimated at 10.6% (95% CI 5.2 to 15.7).
   111	
   112	Table 2 compares the school gates with the boundary road and urban background monitoring
   113	sites.
   114	Table 2. Mean NO2 concentration by monitoring location, January to June, ug/m3
   115	Location type Sites Baseline 2024 Pilot 2025 Change (%)
   116	School gate 12 31.4 26.9 -14.3
   117	Boundary road 8 35.2 35.8 +1.7
   118	Urban background 3 21.6 20.7 -4.2
   119	No school gate site exceeded the annual mean objective of 40 ug/m3 in either period,
   120	although two were within 5 ug/m3 of it at baseline.
   121	The fall at the school gates was seen in every month of the pilot period. It was largest in
   122	February and smallest in June, when concentrations are lowest at all types of site.
   123	4.3 Hourly patterns
   124	Continuous monitors at four schools recorded hourly NO2 concentrations. During the morning
   125	restriction hour, mean NO2 at these four schools was 21% lower than in the baseline period.
   126	The afternoon restriction hour showed a smaller fall of 12%, and outside the restriction
   127	hours the fall was 6%. Because continuous monitors were installed at only four of the twelve
   128	schools, these hourly results may not be representative of all pilot sites.
   129	The concentration of the fall in the restriction hours is consistent with the pilot being
   130	its cause, rather than a general improvement in air quality across the borough.
   131	
   132	4.4 Travel to school
   133	The share of pupils who usually walked, cycled or scooted to school rose from 58% in the
   134	baseline survey to 67% in the pilot survey. These gains were concentrated among pupils
   135	living within one kilometre of the school, while travel by pupils living further away
   136	changed little.
   137	The follow-up survey was completed at only 10 of the 12 schools, because two schools were
   138	unable to run it before the end of term. Baseline results are therefore shown for the same
   139	10 schools.
   140	Table 3. Usual mode of travel to school, percentage of pupils, 10 schools
   141	Mode Baseline March 2024 Pilot March 2025
   142	Walk 49 55
   143	Cycle 3 5
   144	Scooter 6 7
   145	Car 34 25
   146	Bus 6 6
   147	Other 2 2
   148	Parents who had stopped driving most often said that the closure made walking feel safer or
   149	that parking near the school had become more difficult. Some parents reported parking
   150	further away and walking the last part of the journey, which the survey recorded as walking.
   151	
   152	4.5 Traffic on boundary roads
   153	Some drivers who previously used the closed streets diverted to the surrounding main roads.
   154	Across the eight boundary roads, traffic during the restriction hours increased by 6.2%
   155	compared with the baseline period. However, this increase was within the range of normal
   156	year-to-year variation recorded at the borough's permanent traffic counters, which is plus
   157	or minus 8%.
   158	The largest increase, 11%, was on Mill Road next to Crossley Road Primary, where the closed
   159	street had previously carried the most traffic. Outside the restriction hours, traffic on
   160	the boundary roads was unchanged.
   161	4.6 Views of parents and residents
   162	The online survey received 1,206 responses from parents and 388 from residents. Among
   163	parents, 73% supported making the School Street at their child's school permanent, and 18%
   164	were opposed. Among residents, 54% supported a permanent scheme and 37% were opposed.
   165	The resident survey had a response rate of 23%, so these results may not reflect the views
   166	of all residents. Residents who opposed the scheme most often mentioned difficulty with
   167	deliveries and visitors, while supporters most often mentioned quieter streets.
   168	4.7 Enforcement
   169	Penalty charge notices were issued throughout the pilot, but most were issued in the first
   170	half term, and the number fell steadily as drivers became familiar with the closures.
   171	Exemption permits were most often held by residents of the closed streets.
   172	
   173	5 Discussion
   174	The pilot achieved large reductions in motor traffic on the closed streets and a measurable
   175	improvement in air quality at the school gates. The adjusted reduction in NO2 of 10.6% is
   176	smaller than the 23% reported by Rowland and Tait (2021), but their figure referred to the
   177	morning peak only, and our hourly data for the morning restriction hour show a comparable
   178	fall.
   179	The rise in active travel was smaller than in some earlier programmes but was achieved
   180	without volunteer marshals. The evidence of traffic displacement was weak: traffic on
   181	boundary roads rose by a modest amount, and NO2 on those roads was essentially unchanged.
   182	Parental support of 73% is within the range reported by Daley and Moss (2023).
   183	For the council, the main practical lessons concern enforcement and exemptions. Camera
   184	enforcement allowed the closures to operate without staff at the barriers, and a simple
   185	online exemption process kept complaints from residents to a manageable level. Schools on
   186	busier roads, where a closure would divert large volumes of traffic, may need a different
   187	approach.
   188	6 Limitations
   189	The evaluation has several limitations. It used a before-and-after design without control
   190	schools, so other changes between 2024 and 2025 may have contributed to the results,
   191	although the adjustment for background NO2 addresses part of this. Diffusion tubes give
   192	monthly averages and cannot show exposure during the restriction hours at most sites.
   193	The study did not measure health outcomes, such as asthma symptoms or hospital admissions
   194	among pupils, and the pilot period was too short to assess changes in road traffic
   195	collisions. The travel survey relied on pupils' reports of their usual mode of travel and
   196	was not completed at all schools.
   197	
   198	7 Conclusions and recommendations
   199	School Streets reduced motor traffic and NO2 outside the 12 pilot schools and were
   200	associated with more pupils walking, cycling or scooting to school. We recommend that the
   201	council makes the scheme permanent at all 12 schools, continues monitoring on the boundary
   202	roads for a further year, and extends School Streets to suitable schools on the waiting
   203	list.
   204	Acknowledgements
   205	We thank the head teachers, staff, pupils and parents of the 12 pilot schools, the council's
   206	parking enforcement team, and the volunteers who helped to change the diffusion tubes each
   207	month.
   208	Funding
   209	The evaluation was funded by a grant from the Regional Active Travel Fund. The funder had no
   210	role in the design of the evaluation, the analysis or the decision to publish.
   211	References
   212	Abbott J (2020). Changing the school run: results from a 22-school programme. Urban Mobility
   213	Review 6: 100-112.
   214	Daley R, Moss K (2023). Public support for School Streets: a review of 14 evaluations. Urban
   215	Mobility Review 9: 44-58.
   216	Kerrigan P, Shaw L, Udeh C (2022). Traffic displacement near School Streets in northern
   217	England. Transport Policy Studies 31: 210-224.
   218	Pereira A, Lund M (2022). Volunteer-staffed and camera-enforced school streets compared.
   219	Local Transport Research 7: 15-29.
   220	Rowland S, Tait H (2021). Air quality at the school gate: evidence from 37 School Streets.
   221	City Air Quality Journal 4: 77-90.
   222	Data availability
   223	Anonymised traffic counts and diffusion tube results are available from the Transport Policy
   224	and Research Team on request.
   225	Appendix A. Pilot schools
   226	
   227	The 12 pilot schools were Ashgrove Primary, Beckside Primary, Crossley Road Primary, Dunmore
   228	Infant School, Elmfield Primary, Fairholme Junior School, Greystone Primary, Hollins Lane
   229	Primary, Ivydale Primary, Juniper Hill Primary, Kingsmead Primary and Larkrise Primary.
   230	Site-level traffic and NO2 results are held in the accompanying site data workbook.

  p.1 Nurse-Led Discharge Planning on Acute Medical Wards: A Stepped-Wedge Evaluation
  p.1 Evaluation report, September 2025. Department of Nursing Research and Practice Development, Calderbrook General Hospital.
  p.1 Background. Delays in discharging patients who are well enough to leave hospital lengthen hospital stays and reduce the number of beds available for new admissions. We evaluated a nurse-led discharge planning model on six acute medical wards.
  p.1 Methods. The model combined a dedicated discharge coordinator nurse on each ward, an expected date of discharge set within 24 hours of admission, daily board rounds and criteria-led discharge. Wards moved from usual care to the new model in a stepped-wedge sequence between April 2024 and March 2025. The primary outcome was length of stay.
  p.1 Results. The evaluation included 6,948 admissions. Mean length of stay fell from 7.9 to 7.1 days, an adjusted reduction of 0.8 days. Emergency readmission within 30 days was slightly lower in the intervention period, and more patients left hospital before noon.
  p.1 Conclusions. Nurse-led discharge planning shortened hospital stays without an increase in readmissions or deaths. The model could be extended to other wards.
  p.2 Calderbrook General Hospital has operated at more than 95% bed occupancy for most of the past three years. On the acute medical wards, a large share of bed-days is used by patients who are medically fit to leave but are waiting for tests, medicines, transport or support at home. Discharges are often left until late in the day, which delays admissions from the emergency department.
  p.2 National guidance encourages hospitals to plan discharge from the point of admission, to set an expected date of discharge for every patient and to discharge patients earlier in the day. Earlier attempts at Calderbrook to introduce these practices relied on ward managers and medical teams and were not sustained.
  p.2 In 2023 the nursing directorate proposed a nurse-led model of discharge planning, in which a dedicated nurse would take responsibility for preparing each patient's discharge from the day of admission. This report presents the evaluation of that model on six acute medical wards over twelve months.
  p.2 Discharge planning has been studied extensively. A review of 30 randomised trials by Marlow and Ince (2018) found that structured discharge planning reduced mean length of stay by 0.7 days and reduced readmissions at three months, although the effect on readmissions within 30 days was uncertain. Okafor and colleagues (2020) reported that criteria-led discharge reduced mean length of stay by 0.5 days in a cluster trial in eight hospitals, with emergency readmission within 30 days of 12.8% in both arms.

ANSWER: Nurse-led discharge planning reduced length of stay, slightly lowered 30-day readmissions, improved discharge preparedness, and did not increase deaths.

    22	home. Discharges are often left until late in the day, which delays admissions from the
    23	emergency department.
    24	National guidance encourages hospitals to plan discharge from the point of admission, to set
    25	an expected date of discharge for every patient and to discharge patients earlier in the
    26	day. Earlier attempts at Calderbrook to introduce these practices relied on ward managers
    27	and medical teams and were not sustained.
    28	In 2023 the nursing directorate proposed a nurse-led model of discharge planning, in which a
    29	dedicated nurse would take responsibility for preparing each patient's discharge from the
    30	day of admission. This report presents the evaluation of that model on six acute medical
    31	wards over twelve months.
    32	2 Literature review
    33	Discharge planning has been studied extensively. A review of 30 randomised trials by Marlow
    34	and Ince (2018) found that structured discharge planning reduced mean length of stay by 0.7
    35	days and reduced readmissions at three months, although the effect on readmissions within 30
    36	days was uncertain. Okafor and colleagues (2020) reported that criteria-led discharge
    37	reduced mean length of stay by 0.5 days in a cluster trial in eight hospitals, with
    38	emergency readmission within 30 days of 12.8% in both arms.
    39	Other studies have focused on the timing of discharge. Lindqvist (2021) found that the share
    40	of patients discharged before noon rose from 15% to 24% after daily board rounds were
    41	introduced in a teaching hospital. The workload implications are less clear: Prescott (2019)
    42	estimated that nurse-led discharge required 31 minutes of additional registered nurse time
    43	per patient, while Haddad and Byrne (2022) found no change in overtime hours.
    44	Few studies have evaluated a combined model in a district general hospital, and fewer still
    45	have measured both patient outcomes and nursing time.
    46	
    47	3 Methods
    48	3.1 Setting and design
    49	The evaluation took place on six acute medical wards with a total of 168 beds. We used a
    50	stepped-wedge design: all wards began in the control period, and one ward moved to the
    51	intervention every two months, in an order chosen by lottery, until all six wards were using
    52	the new model.
    53	3.2 The intervention
    54	Each ward appointed a discharge coordinator, a band 6 registered nurse working on weekdays,
    55	funded at 1.0 whole-time equivalent per ward. The coordinator set an expected date of
    56	discharge within 24 hours of admission, led a daily board round at 09:00, arranged
    57	medicines, transport and community referrals, and authorised criteria-led discharge when
    58	agreed clinical criteria were met. Ward managers and coordinators received two half-day
    59	training sessions before each ward moved to the intervention.
    60	3.3 Outcomes
    61	The primary outcome was length of stay in days. Secondary outcomes were emergency
    62	readmission within 30 days, death within 30 days of discharge, the proportion of patients
    63	discharged before noon, and bed-days lost to delayed discharge. Patients completed a
    64	readiness for discharge questionnaire, scored from 0 to 10, on the day of discharge.
    65	Nursing time was measured by work sampling on two randomly chosen days each month. Ward
    66	staff nurses were invited to complete an anonymous workload survey in March 2025.
    67	3.4 Analysis
    68	Outcomes were compared between control and intervention periods using mixed-effects models
    69	with a random effect for ward and a fixed effect for calendar month, to allow for seasonal
    70	trends. Results are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and a significance level of
    71	0.05 was specified in advance.
    72	3.5 Data sources
    73	Admission, discharge and readmission data were taken from the hospital's patient
    74	administration system. Deaths after discharge were identified through the national death
    75	register, and delayed discharges were taken from the daily ward status return.
    76	3.6 Patient and public involvement
    77	
    78	Two former patients and a carer sat on the evaluation steering group. They helped to word
    79	the readiness for discharge questionnaire and advised on how to approach patients on the day
    80	of discharge.
    81	
    82	4 Results
    83	4.1 Participants
    84	The evaluation included 6,948 admissions of adults aged 18 and over: 3,302 during control
    85	periods and 3,646 during intervention periods. Patient characteristics were similar in the
    86	two periods (Table 1).
    87	Table 1. Characteristics of admissions by study period
    88	Characteristic Control period Intervention period
    89	Admissions 3,302 3,646
    90	Mean age, years 74.1 73.8
    91	Women, % 52 51
    92	Admitted through the emergency department, % 88 89
    93	Living alone, % 34 33
    94	Aged 80 and over, % 32 32
    95	4.2 Length of stay
    96	Mean length of stay was 7.9 days in the control period and 7.1 days in the intervention
    97	period. After adjustment for ward and calendar month, the new model reduced mean length of
    98	stay by 0.8 days (95% CI 0.5 to 1.1). Table 2 summarises the primary and secondary outcomes.
    99	Table 2. Primary and secondary outcomes by study period
   100	Outcome Control period Intervention period Adjusted effect (95% CI)
   101	Mean length of stay, days 7.9 7.1 -0.8 days (-1.1 to -0.5)
   102	Emergency readmission within 30 days, % 15.1 14.2 OR 0.93 (0.79 to 1.09)
   103	Discharged before noon, % 18.6 29.3 OR 1.84 (1.58 to 2.14)
   104	Death within 30 days of discharge, % 5.4 5.2 OR 0.97 (0.80 to 1.18)
   105	Readiness for discharge score, 0 to 10 6.8 7.4 +0.6 (0.3 to 0.9)
   106	
   107	4.3 Readmissions and mortality
   108	Emergency readmission within 30 days occurred after 14.2% of discharges in the intervention
   109	period and 15.1% of discharges in the control period (adjusted odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.79
   110	to 1.09). However, the difference was not statistically significant. Mortality within 30
   111	days of discharge was similar in the two periods (Table 2). The most common reasons for
   112	readmission in both periods were respiratory infection, heart failure and urinary infection.
   113	4.4 Discharge timing and delays
   114	The proportion of patients leaving hospital before noon rose under the new model (Table 2).
   115	Bed-days lost to delayed discharge, counted from the day a patient was recorded as medically
   116	fit to leave, fell from 1,184 in the control period to 902 in the intervention period. This
   117	fall was driven mainly by quicker arrangement of medicines to take home and of transport.
   118	4.5 Readiness for discharge
   119	Patients discharged under the new model reported feeling better prepared to leave hospital.
   120	The mean readiness for discharge score rose from 6.8 to 7.4 out of 10. Questionnaires were
   121	returned by 61% of patients, and the return rate was lower among patients aged 80 and over.
   122	
   123	4.6 Results by age group
   124	The effect of the new model differed by age (Table 3). Among patients aged 80 years and
   125	over, mean length of stay fell by 1.4 days, from 10.4 to 9.0 days. This effect was almost
   126	three times the reduction seen in patients under 80, whose length of stay fell by 0.5 days.
   127	The subgroup analysis was exploratory and had not been specified in the study protocol.
   128	Table 3. Mean length of stay in days by age group and study period
   129	Age group Control period Intervention period Difference
   130	18 to 64 5.6 5.3 -0.3
   131	65 to 79 7.6 6.9 -0.7
   132	80 and over 10.4 9.0 -1.4
   133	All ages 7.9 7.1 -0.8
   134	Patients aged 80 and over made up 32% of admissions but accounted for 42% of bed-days in the
   135	control period. Most of the additional reduction in this group came from fewer days spent
   136	waiting for care packages at home.
   137	
   138	4.7 Nursing time and workload
   139	Work sampling showed that discharge coordinators spent a mean of 26 minutes on each
   140	discharge, covering board rounds, referrals, medicines and contact with families. Time spent
   141	by ward staff nurses on discharge paperwork fell from 52 to 34 minutes per shift.
   142	In the staff survey, 64% of ward nurses said that their workload was about the same as or
   143	lighter than before the new model, and 22% said it was heavier. Only 41% of ward nurses
   144	returned the survey, so these views may not be representative of all ward staff.
   145	4.8 Implementation
   146	An expected date of discharge was recorded within 24 hours for 87% of admissions in the
   147	intervention period, and board rounds took place on 94% of weekdays. Criteria-led discharge
   148	was used for 19% of discharges, most often at weekends when no senior doctor was on the
   149	ward.
   150	5 Discussion
   151	The nurse-led model shortened hospital stays by a margin similar to that reported in earlier
   152	trials, and the largest gains were among patients aged 80 and over, who occupy the most
   153	bed-days. These gains came without an increase in readmissions or deaths.
   154	The reduction of 0.8 days is close to the 0.7 days reported in the review by Marlow and Ince
   155	(2018), and larger than the 0.5 days found for criteria-led discharge alone by Okafor and
   156	colleagues (2020). The rise in discharges before noon was larger than in earlier reports,
   157	which suggests that the daily board round was an important part of the model.
   158	The workload findings need careful interpretation. The time saved by ward staff nurses was
   159	largely offset by the time spent by the coordinators, so the model redistributed discharge
   160	work to a dedicated role rather than reducing total nursing time.
   161	
   162	6 Limitations
   163	This was a single-site evaluation, and ward staff could not be blinded to the intervention.
   164	Although the stepped-wedge design and adjustment for calendar month reduce the influence of
   165	seasonal trends, other changes during the year, such as new community care contracts, may
   166	have contributed to shorter stays. We did not undertake an economic evaluation, so the costs
   167	of the coordinator posts have not been compared with the value of the bed-days saved.
   168	7 Conclusions
   169	Nurse-led discharge planning reduced length of stay on acute medical wards without
   170	increasing readmissions. The hospital should consider extending the model to the remaining
   171	medical wards, with continued monitoring of readmissions and staff workload.
   172	Acknowledgements
   173	We thank the ward managers, discharge coordinators and patients who took part, and the
   174	hospital's information team for extracting admission data.
   175	Ethics and data availability
   176	The evaluation was registered as a service evaluation with the hospital's clinical audit
   177	department, and research ethics committee review was not required. Patients could decline
   178	the readiness questionnaire without any effect on their care. Aggregate data are available
   179	from the Department of Nursing Research on request.
   180	Funding and conflicts of interest
   181	The evaluation was funded by the Calderbrook Hospital Charity. The authors are employed by
   182	the hospital, and two of the authors helped to design the nurse-led model.

   188	Marlow T, Ince G (2018). Structured discharge planning: a review of 30 randomised trials.
   189	Review of Hospital Care 22: 140-161.
   190	Okafor U, Brennan J, Silva M (2020). Criteria-led discharge in eight hospitals: a cluster
   191	
   192	trial. Acute Medicine Research 14: 201-213.

   194	57-66.
     1	Board Briefing: Nurse-Led Discharge Planning on Acute Medical Wards
     2	
     3	For the Trust Board meeting on 6 November 2025. Prepared by the Office of the Chief Nurse. For decision.
     4	
     5	Purpose
     6	
     7	This paper summarises the evaluation of the nurse-led discharge planning model that ran on six acute medical wards between April 2024 and March 2025, and asks the Board to approve extending the model.
     8	
     9	Background
    10	
    11	The acute medical wards have run at more than 95% bed occupancy for most of the last three years, and delays in discharge are a major cause of long waits for beds in the emergency department. The nurse-led model was designed to plan each discharge from the day of admission, with a dedicated coordinator nurse on every ward.
    12	
    13	Key findings
    14	
    15	The evaluation covered 6,948 admissions. Under the new model, the average hospital stay was 1.2 days shorter, which is equivalent to freeing several beds every day across the six wards.
    16	
    17	Readmissions within 30 days fell from 15.1% to 14.2%, and patients reported feeling better prepared to go home. Patients aged 80 and over benefited most.
    18	
    19	Ward nurses now spend less time on discharge paperwork, and most nurses who responded to the staff survey said their workload was the same or lighter.
    20	
    21	Resources
    22	
    23	The model requires one discharge coordinator nurse per ward. The six coordinator posts are funded from the hospital charity grant until March 2026. No savings have yet been calculated, and Finance will develop the economic case for the Board in early 2026.
    24	
    25	Recommendation
    26	
    27	The Board is asked to approve extending nurse-led discharge planning to the four remaining medical wards from April 2026, subject to the economic case.
    28	
    29	Risks
    30	
    31	The main risks are recruiting experienced band 6 nurses to the coordinator posts and keeping daily board rounds going during periods of high demand.
    32	
    33	Next steps
    34	
    35	If the Board approves the extension, recruitment to the four new coordinator posts will begin in January 2026, and the Chief Nurse will report progress to the Quality Committee every quarter.
results.answer:
The evaluation found that nurse-led discharge planning:

- shortened hospital stays on the acute medical wards
- reduced mean length of stay from 7.9 to 7.1 days, an adjusted reduction of 0.8 days
- did not increase emergency readmissions or deaths
- increased the proportion of patients discharged before noon
- improved patients’ reported readiness for discharge
- reduced ward nurses’ time on discharge paperwork, while shifting some work to the discharge coordinator role

It also found the biggest benefit in patients aged 80 and over.

ANSWER: Nurse-led discharge planning reduced length of stay by 0.8 days without increasing readmissions or deaths, improved discharge timing and patient readiness, and shifted some discharge work from ward nurses to dedicated coordinator nurses.

The report says the new discharge approach did **not clearly pile more work onto ward nurses overall**.

Relevant findings:
- “Time spent by ward staff nurses on discharge paperwork fell from **52 to 34 minutes per shift**.”
- In the staff survey, “**64%** of ward nurses said that their workload was about the same as or lighter than before the new model, and **22%** said it was heavier.”
- The discussion notes that “the time saved by ward staff nurses was largely offset by the time spent by the coordinators,” so the model “redistributed discharge work to a dedicated role rather than reducing total nursing time.”

So, according to the evaluation, ward nurses’ discharge paperwork burden decreased, but total nursing time was mostly shifted to the discharge coordinators rather than eliminated.

ANSWER: No overall—it reduced ward nurses’ discharge paperwork time from “52 to 34 minutes per shift,” and most nurses said workload was “about the same as or lighter,” though total discharge work was largely shifted to the coordinators rather than removed.

results.answer:
No, not overall. The evaluation says:

- “64% of ward nurses said that their workload was about the same as or lighter than before the new model, and 22% said it was heavier.”
- It also says the model “redistributed discharge work to a dedicated role rather than reducing total nursing time.”

So the new discharge approach did not clearly pile more work onto ward nurses, though a minority did report heavier workload.

ANSWER: Mostly no — most ward nurses reported the same or lighter workload, though 22% said it was heavier, and the work was mainly redistributed rather than eliminated.

Yes — the 30-day readmission rate fell slightly, from "15.1%" in the control period to "14.2%" in the intervention period. The evaluation says the adjusted odds ratio was "0.93 (0.79 to 1.09)" and that the difference "was not statistically significant."

ANSWER: Yes, slightly: 30-day readmissions fell from 15.1% to 14.2%, but the difference was not statistically significant.
